exploreAction.instruction: Read how the peregrine falcon tucks its wings into a teardrop and stoops at over 300 km/h, making it the fastest animal on the planet. Explore how its nictitating membranes protect the eyes at speed, how it knocks prey out of the sky with a closed talon, and why cities full of pigeons have become its favorite hunting ground.

name: Arctic Tern
teaser: The animal that migrates the farthest on Earth

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the arctic tern migrates from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back each year, covering up to 90,000 km and seeing more daylight than any other animal. Explore how these tiny birds navigate by the sun, stars, and magnetic field, and why they chase endless summer across the globe.

name: Hummingbird
teaser: The only bird that can fly backwards

exploreAction.instruction: Read how hummingbirds beat their wings up to 80 times a second, hover in place, and even fly backwards, powered by nectar they lap up at up to 15 licks a second. Explore their sky-high metabolism, torpor at night to save energy, and how their iridescent feathers flash color from tiny air pockets, not pigment.

name: Emperor Penguin
teaser: The penguin that breeds through the Antarctic winter

exploreAction.instruction: Read how emperor penguins breed during the darkest, coldest months of the Antarctic winter, with males incubating the single egg on their feet under a brood pouch while females travel up to 100 km to feed. Explore how they huddle against minus 60 degrees, and how fathers survive months without eating.

name: Ostrich
teaser: The biggest and fastest bird on land

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the ostrich traded flight for speed, using two-toed legs that can sprint at 70 km/h and deliver a dangerous kick. Explore its eyes, bigger than its brain, its communal nests, and the myth of burying its head in the sand, which it never actually does.

name: Bald Eagle
teaser: The American symbol with a surprising cry

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the bald eagle, the US national bird, builds the largest tree nests of any bird, up to 4 meters deep and weighing over a ton. Explore how its 240 degree field of vision and talons with 400 psi grip make it a master fisher, and the famous myth that its cry is a hawk's, borrowed in Hollywood films.

name: Macaw
teaser: The colorful parrot with a human-like voice

exploreAction.instruction: Read how macaws crack open Brazil nuts with beaks that can crush a coconut, eat clay to neutralize toxins, and form lifelong pair bonds, sometimes living 50 years in the wild. Explore their intelligence, their loud screeching flocks, and how some mimic human speech and even understand what they say.

name: Kiwi
teaser: The flightless bird that acts like a mammal

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the kiwi, New Zealand's national bird, has tiny useless wings, whiskers like a cat, and lays an egg a quarter of its own body weight, the largest egg relative to body size of any bird. Explore how it hunts by smell at night, and why it behaves more like a small mammal than a bird.

name: Peacock
teaser: The bird with the famous shimmering train

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the peacock's train of up to 200 feathers is not its tail but elongated coverts, shimmering with structural color that shifts as it moves. Explore why females choose mates on the quality of these eyespots, how the display fans out and rattles, and the heavy price males pay dragging this ornament around.

name: Swift
teaser: The bird that lives its life in the air

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the common swift can stay airborne for up to 10 months, eating, sleeping, and even mating on the wing, only landing to nest. Explore how it drinks by skimming water, sleeps with half its brain awake, and racks up millions of kilometers in a lifetime.

name: Cassowary
teaser: The rainforest bird called the most dangerous

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the cassowary of New Guinea and northern Australia is often called the world's most dangerous bird, kicking with 12 cm dagger-like claws on its inner toes. Explore how it swallows rainforest fruits whole and spreads seeds, earning the title of forest gardener, and why it's a living reminder of dinosaurs.

name: Flamingo
teaser: The pink bird that eats backwards

exploreAction.instruction: Read how flamingos get their pink from carotenoid pigments in the algae and shrimp they filter, and how their upside-down feeding with a tongue acting like a pump separates food from mud. Explore their one-legged standing habit, still not fully explained, and their huge noisy breeding colonies of millions.

name: Hornbill
teaser: The bird that seals itself in a tree to raise chicks

exploreAction.instruction: Read how female hornbills seal themselves inside tree cavities with mud, leaving only a slit through which males pass food, to protect chicks from predators. Explore the casque on top of the beak, its role in calls and courtship, and how some hornbills use the same nest hole for decades.

name: Secretary Bird
teaser: The snake-hunter with eyelashes

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the secretary bird of African savannas hunts snakes by stomping them with powerful kicks of up to 195 Newtons, delivered in rapid succession. Explore its long eyelash-like feathers, its name from the quill pens behind 19th-century secretaries' ears, and its habit of walking up to 20 km a day on foot.

name: Toco Toucan
teaser: The bird with a bill longer than its body

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the toco toucan's huge orange bill, up to a third of its length, is surprisingly light, made of keratin over a honeycomb of bone, and works as a radiator to shed heat. Explore how it tosses fruit with the bill and catches it, and why the bill's size is a display of fitness.

name: Resplendent Quetzal
teaser: The sacred bird of the cloud forest

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the resplendent quetzal, sacred to the Maya and Aztecs, trails tail feathers up to 65 cm long from its back, molting them only after nesting. Explore why it was worshipped as the god Quetzalcoatl, why killing one was a capital crime, and its dependence on cloud forests with wild avocado trees.

name: Golden Eagle
teaser: The mountain hunter that takes down deer

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the golden eagle hunts from a mile up, folding into a stoop that can exceed 240 km/h, and has been recorded killing foxes, goats, and even young deer. Explore its pair bond that lasts a lifetime, its enormous eyries reused for generations, and its use in falconry for thousands of years.

name: Pelican
teaser: The bird with the built-in fishing net

exploreAction.instruction: Read how pelicans scoop fish with a throat pouch that can hold 13 liters of water, then drain it and swallow. Explore their coordinated fishing in flocks, the myth of carrying fish in the pouch (they don't), and how chicks feed by reaching into the parent's pouch.

name: Albatross
teaser: The seabird that never lands for years

exploreAction.instruction: Read how albatrosses use dynamic soaring to travel 10,000 km without flapping, locking their wings with a tendon so muscles never tire. Explore how they sleep on the wing, drink seawater through a salt gland, and how plastic pollution now threatens them at sea.

name: Kingfisher
teaser: The bird that dives like an arrow

exploreAction.instruction: Read how kingfishers spot fish from a branch, hover, then plunge headfirst with eyes shielded by a nictitating membrane, rarely missing. Explore how the shape of their beak inspired bullet-train nose design in Japan, and why their feathers can appear blue without any blue pigment.

name: Kookaburra
teaser: The bird whose laugh sounds human

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the kookaburra's territorial call sounds like a raucous human laugh, sung in chorus at dawn and dusk across Australia. Explore how it hunts snakes, lizards, and insects with a heavy beak, nests in hollows, and why its laugh is used in movies to set jungle scenes, even in Africa.

name: Blue-footed Booby
teaser: The bird that dances for a mate

exploreAction.instruction: Read how male blue-footed boobies show off bright blue feet in an elaborate high-stepping dance, with females choosing mates by the blueness of the pigment derived from fresh fish. Explore their dive-bombing fishing style, their clumsy name, and the sky-pointing greeting ritual of pairs.

name: Ruby-throated Hummingbird Migration
teaser: The 800 km nonstop flight of a 3 gram bird

exploreAction.instruction: Read how ruby-throated hummingbirds, weighing about the same as a coin, fatten up and fly nonstop across the Gulf of Mexico, some 800 km of open water. Explore how they almost double their weight beforehand, how scientists confirmed the crossing, and the risks of storms and exhaustion.

name: Lyrebird
teaser: The bird that mimics chainsaws and camera shutters

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the superb lyrebird can imitate almost any sound, from other birds to camera shutters, car alarms, and chainsaws, learned from its environment. Explore its spectacular tail shaped like a lyre, its complex courtship display on dancing mounds, and how males can sing for hours with near-perfect pitch.

name: Woodpecker
teaser: The bird that drums on trees without brain damage

exploreAction.instruction: Read how woodpeckers strike wood up to 20 times a second with forces over a thousand times gravity, protected by a spongy skull, a shock-absorbing tongue wrapped around the brain, and a chisel beak that self-sharpens. Explore how their drumming signals territory and how they dig nest cavities in seconds.

name: King Penguin
teaser: The penguin with the slowest breeding cycle

exploreAction.instruction: Read how king penguins take 14 to 16 months to raise a single chick, breeding on sub-Antarctic islands with a crowded crèche system where parents find their own chick by call. Explore their teardrop shape for swimming, diving past 300 meters, and their bright orange ear patches.

name: Snowy Owl
teaser: The white owl of the Arctic tundra

exploreAction.instruction: Read how snowy owls breed on the Arctic tundra, nesting on the ground in sync with lemming booms, and hunt around the clock under the midnight sun. Explore how their white feathers provide camouflage, their yellow eyes, and how hungry years send them irrupting far south.

name: Vulture
teaser: The recycler of the savanna

exploreAction.instruction: Read how vultures soar for hours on thermals, spotting carcasses from kilometers away, and strip a body within hours, saving the ecosystem from disease. Explore their bald heads for hygiene, stomach acid that kills anthrax and botulism, and how poisoning and drugs nearly wiped out Asian vultures.

name: Puffin
teaser: The clown of the sea that nests underground

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Atlantic puffins spend the winter at sea, then return to cliff-top burrows they dig with beaks and feet, carrying up to 60 fish at once held crosswise by a spiny tongue. Explore their colorful breeding beaks that shed in winter, and how they mate for life and return to the same burrow.

name: Condor
teaser: The vulture with a three meter wingspan

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Andean condor, one of the largest flying birds, weighs up to 15 kg and soars on mountain updrafts with a wingspan over 3 meters, barely flapping. Explore its bald head, its near-extinction and captive breeding comeback, and how it can live over 70 years in the wild.

name: Shoebill
teaser: The prehistoric-looking swamp hunter

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the shoebill of African papyrus swamps stands motionless for hours like a statue, then strikes with its enormous shoe-shaped bill to grab lungfish and even baby crocodiles. Explore its unsettling stare, its bill-clattering greeting, and why it's considered a living fossil.

name: Bee-eater
teaser: The acrobat that eats stinging insects

exploreAction.instruction: Read how bee-eaters catch bees and wasps mid-flight, rub them against a branch to remove the sting, and eat them. Explore their dazzling rainbow colors, their underground nest tunnels dug into riverbanks, and how they avoid being stung through repeated rubbing and squeezing.

name: Andean Cock-of-the-rock
teaser: The flame-orange bird of cloud forests

exploreAction.instruction: Read how male Andean cocks-of-the-rock, vivid orange with a fan-shaped crest, gather on jungle leks to dance and display for females. Explore the lek mating system, the female's brown camouflage for nesting on cliff faces, and why Peru made it its national bird.

name: Avocet
teaser: The wading bird with the upturned beak

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the avocet sweeps its uniquely upturned bill side to side through shallow water to catch tiny crustaceans. Explore its striking black and white plumage, its breeding colonies on salt flats, and how it defends nests with a furious distraction display.

name: Great Horned Owl
teaser: The tiger of the sky

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the great horned owl hunts at night with hearing so acute it can strike prey under snow, its serrated feather edges make flight silent, and its grip can crush a rabbit's spine. Explore why it's called the tiger of the sky, taking prey from mice to skunks, and its deep resonant hooting.

name: Magnificent Frigatebird
teaser: The pirate of the skies that can't swim

exploreAction.instruction: Read how frigatebirds spend weeks soaring over tropical oceans, too waterlogged to swim, snatching fish from the surface and robbing other seabirds mid-air. Explore how males inflate a huge red throat pouch to attract females, and how they sleep with half a brain while soaring.

name: Jabiru Stork
teaser: The giant stork of the Pantanal

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the jabiru stork of South American wetlands stands up to 1.5 meters tall with a black neck and massive bill, wading for fish and small animals. Explore its huge stick nests reused for years, its silent flight, and how it's a flagship of the Pantanal.

name: Gouldian Finch
teaser: The rainbow finch of Australia

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Gouldian finch of northern Australia flashes red, black, yellow, purple, and turquoise in one small body, with heads in three color morphs that once were traded as separate species. Explore its seed diet, its seasonal nesting in tree hollows, and threats from fire and trapping.

name: Emperor Penguin Deep Dives
teaser: The dive that goes 500 meters deep

exploreAction.instruction: Read how emperor penguins dive deeper than any other bird, past 500 meters, holding their breath for over 20 minutes, with muscles that work on stored oxygen and a heart rate that drops to a few beats a minute. Explore how they hunt fish and squid in the dark depths and return to breathe through breathing holes in the ice.

name: Kestrel
teaser: The falcon that hovers like a helicopter

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the kestrel hovers almost motionless by facing into the wind, adjusting its head with tiny movements to keep perfectly still while scanning for voles, and can even see ultraviolet light to spot mouse urine trails. Explore why it's one of the most adaptable birds of prey.

name: Cockatoo
teaser: The crested parrot that dances to music

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sulphur-crested cockatoos lift their dramatic yellow crests in emotion, live up to 80 years, and have been seen dancing in rhythm to music, an ability once thought unique to humans. Explore their loud flocks, their tool use with sticks, and their habit of learning to open bins.

name: Kingfisher Family
teaser: The global family from fish to snakes

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the kingfisher family spans 120 species worldwide, from tiny African dwarf kingfishers that catch insects to the giant kookaburra that hunts snakes, proving the name undersells their varied diet. Explore how some dive for fish while others hunt on land, and how they dig nest tunnels.

name: Purple Martin
teaser: The swallow that depends on human housing

exploreAction.instruction: Read how purple martins in North America now nest almost entirely in human-made gourds and apartments, a relationship that goes back to Indigenous peoples hanging hollow gourds centuries ago. Explore their acrobatic insect-catching, their communal roosts of hundreds of thousands, and their full migration to South America.

name: Horned Lizard
teaser: The lizard that squirts blood from its eyes

exploreAction.instruction: Read how horned lizards defend against canids by squirting blood from their eye ducts up to 1.5 meters, the blood laced with chemicals that repel dogs and coyotes. Explore their flattened bodies, their armor of scales and horns, and their favorite food, harvester ants.

name: Komodo Dragon
teaser: The giant lizard with a venomous bite

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Komodo dragon, the largest living lizard at up to 3 meters, hunts with serrated teeth and venom glands that lower blood pressure and prevent clotting, weakening prey over days. Explore how it senses carrion from kilometers away, and how it attacks everything from deer to water buffalo.

name: Chameleon
teaser: The lizard that shoots its tongue like a catapult

exploreAction.instruction: Read how chameleons catch prey by shooting a tongue longer than their body at 26 body lengths a second, and change color not mainly for camouflage but for mood, temperature, and signaling. Explore their independently rotating eyes, their grasping feet, and how color change happens in skin cell nanocrystals.

name: Gecko
teaser: The lizard that sticks to glass

exploreAction.instruction: Read how geckos climb smooth glass using millions of microscopic hairs called setae that create van der Waals forces, enough to hold 130 kg in theory. Explore their tails that drop off, their toe pads that self-clean, and how this biology inspired real climbing robots and adhesives.

name: Green Anaconda
teaser: The heaviest snake on Earth

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the green anaconda of South American rivers can weigh over 200 kg and reach 9 meters, constricting prey with pressure that stops blood flow within minutes. Explore its aquatic life, eyes and nostrils on top of the head, and how females are far larger than males.

name: King Cobra
teaser: The snake that builds a nest and guards it

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the king cobra, the world's longest venomous snake, is the only snake that builds a nest, the female coiling leaves into a mound and guarding it until eggs hatch. Explore how it feeds almost entirely on other snakes, its hood and hiss, and why its venom is a neurotoxin that can kill an elephant.

name: Gila Monster
teaser: The venomous lizard with a beaded skin

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Gila monster is one of only two venomous lizards, gripping and chewing venom into wounds with grooved teeth, and how its venom inspired the diabetes drug exenatide. Explore its slow desert life, its fat-storing tail, and how it can survive months between meals.

name: Alligator Snapping Turtle
teaser: The turtle that fishes with its tongue

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the alligator snapping turtle lies motionless on riverbeds, wiggling a worm-like lure on its tongue to draw in fish, then snaps shut with jaws that can sever a finger. Explore its armor of heavy plates, its legendary size, and how it rarely moves for years.

name: Galapagos Tortoise
teaser: The giant that lives over 150 years

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Galapagos tortoises can exceed 150 years and weigh over 400 kg, storing water and fat to survive months without food or drink. Explore the island-specific shell shapes Darwin noted, the near-extinction from whalers, and the breeding programs that brought species back.

name: Crocodile
teaser: The ambush predator unchanged for 200 million years

exploreAction.instruction: Read how crocodiles have survived for over 200 million years with a bite force of 3,700 psi, the strongest of any animal, yet jaw muscles so weak you can hold them shut. Explore how they sense ripples with face pressure receptors, swallow stones as ballast, and care for their young.

name: Frilled Lizard
teaser: The lizard with a built-in umbrella

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the frilled lizard of Australia and New Guinea erects a large frill around its neck to startle predators, gaping its mouth and hissing, then runs off on two legs. Explore how the frill is also used in courtship and temperature control, and its habit of fleeing up trees.

name: Green Sea Turtle
teaser: The ocean traveler that returns to its birth beach

exploreAction.instruction: Read how green sea turtles migrate thousands of kilometers between feeding grounds and nesting beaches, with females returning to lay eggs on the exact beach where they hatched decades earlier. Explore how they navigate by magnetic fields, why hatchlings race to the sea, and threats from plastic and light pollution.

name: Black Mamba
teaser: The fastest and most feared African snake

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the black mamba, Africa's longest venomous snake at up to 4.5 meters, moves at up to 20 km/h with a neurotoxic venom that can kill within 20 minutes untreated. Explore why its name comes from the black inside of its mouth, and how it prefers to flee, striking only when cornered.

name: Basilisk Lizard
teaser: The lizard that runs on water

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the green basilisk lizard of Central America sprints across water on its hind legs, using the speed and slap of its feet and air pockets under its toes to stay above the surface for several meters. Explore how juveniles can run farther than adults, and its crests that earned the Jesus lizard nickname.

name: Tuatara
teaser: The living relic with a third eye

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the tuatara of New Zealand is the last survivor of a reptile order that died out elsewhere 60 million years ago, carrying a light-sensing third eye on its forehead. Explore its slow metabolism that lets it live over 100 years, its slow growth, and how it outlives the dinosaurs' end.

name: Mata-mata Turtle
teaser: The leaf-like ambush hunter

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the mata-mata turtle of South America looks like a pile of dead leaves, with a flattened shell, fringed skin, and a snorkel-like snout. Explore how it opens its huge mouth to suck in fish like a vacuum, and how its disguise lets it vanish in muddy water.

name: Desert Iguana
teaser: The lizard that runs on hot sand

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the desert iguana of the American Southwest tolerates body temperatures above 46 degrees Celsius, scurrying between shrubs in the midday heat that stops other animals. Explore its salt-excreting nasal glands, its diet of creosote flowers, and how it raises its body off hot sand.

name: Monitor Lizard
teaser: The intelligent hunter of the lizard world

exploreAction.instruction: Read how monitor lizards, including the water monitor and lace monitor, are among the most intelligent reptiles, able to count, learn tasks, and remember people, with a forked tongue that samples the air. Explore their claws for climbing and digging, their swimming ability, and how they scavenge and hunt.

name: Caiman
teaser: The armored crocodilian of the Americas

exploreAction.instruction: Read how caimans, smaller relatives of crocodiles and alligators, thrive across South America, with the black caiman reaching 5 meters in the Amazon. Explore their armored belly scales used for leather, how mothers carry hatchlings in their jaws, and their role in dry-season pools.

name: Leaf-tailed Gecko
teaser: The gecko that disappears as bark

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Madagascar's leaf-tailed geckos flatten their bodies against tree trunks, their tails shaped like decaying leaves, their camouflage so perfect they're nearly impossible to spot by day. Explore their huge lidless eyes for night hunting, their color that matches specific bark, and their threatened habitat.

name: Reticulated Python
teaser: The longest snake on Earth

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the reticulated python of Southeast Asia is the longest snake, with verified specimens over 7 meters and folklore of longer ones, a constrictor that climbs trees and hunts mammals and birds. Explore its beautiful diamond pattern, its heat-sensing labial pits, and how females coil around eggs to incubate them.

name: Viper
teaser: The fanged hunter with heat vision

exploreAction.instruction: Read how vipers, from adders to rattlesnakes, hunt with long hollow fangs that fold back, and pit vipers sense infrared heat through facial pits to strike warm prey in total darkness. Explore how their venom ranges from hemotoxins to neurotoxins, how they hiss and warn, and how newborns are born live with working fangs.

name: Axolotl
teaser: The salamander that never grows up

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the axolotl keeps its juvenile gills and stays aquatic for life, a phenomenon called neoteny, and can regenerate lost limbs, spinal cords, and even parts of its heart and brain. Explore why it lives only in the canals of Mexico City, its Xochimilco habitat, and its role in regeneration research.

name: Poison Dart Frog
teaser: The tiny frog with potent skin toxins

exploreAction.instruction: Read how poison dart frogs pack enough toxin in their skin to kill predators, the most toxic species carrying enough to kill ten humans, the poison used by Indigenous hunters on blow darts. Explore how their bright colors warn predators, and the mystery that frogs raised in captivity lose their toxicity.

name: Red-eyed Tree Frog
teaser: The frog with the famous bulging eyes

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the red-eyed tree frog of Central American rainforests sleeps flattened on leaves, hidden by green skin, then flashes startling red eyes and orange feet to startle predators when disturbed. Explore its gelatinous egg masses over water, the race of tadpoles to the pond, and its night insect hunts.

name: Salamander
teaser: The lizard-like amphibian that regrows limbs

exploreAction.instruction: Read how salamanders can regrow complete limbs, tails, jaws, and even parts of the heart and brain, a regeneration superpower scientists study to help human healing. Explore their moist skin breathing, the difference from lizards, and the giant Japanese and Chinese salamanders that reach 1.8 meters.

name: African Bullfrog
teaser: The frog that burrows and waits for years

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the African bullfrog survives drought by burrowing up to a meter deep, shedding a watertight cocoon of skin, and staying dormant for years until rains come. Explore its legendary aggression, its appetite for anything it can swallow, and how males guard tadpoles by digging channels.

name: Tree Frog
teaser: The frog that sticks to leaves with suction pads

exploreAction.instruction: Read how tree frogs cling to smooth leaves and glass with adhesive toe pads covered in hexagonal cells, and glide between trees with oversized webbed feet in some species. Explore their diverse calls from trills to whistles, their bright colors and camouflage, and how many change color to match surroundings.

name: Hellbender
teaser: The giant salamander of American rivers

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the hellbender, North America's largest salamander at up to 74 cm, lives under rocks in fast Appalachian rivers, breathing through its wrinkled skin. Explore how it got the nickname snot otter from its slimy mucus, how males guard nests, and why it's a sensitive indicator of clean water.

name: Surinam Toad
teaser: The toad that hatches babies from its back

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Surinam toad embeds its eggs into the spongy skin of the female's back, where they develop into fully formed toadlets that burst out, a strategy found nowhere else. Explore its flattened leaf-like body, its star-tipped fingers for sensing prey in murky water, and its bizarre underwater life.

name: Wood Frog
teaser: The frog that freezes solid and survives

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the wood frog of Alaska and Canada freezes up to 65 percent of its body water solid in winter, its heart and breathing stopping for months, then thaws out and hops away in spring. Explore the cryoprotectant glucose in its blood, how scientists studied the thaw, and why it's a freeze-tolerance champion.

name: Fire-bellied Toad
teaser: The toad that flashes a warning belly

exploreAction.instruction: Read how fire-bellied toads, when threatened, arch their bodies and flash bright red or orange bellies in a pose called the unken reflex, warning predators of skin toxins. Explore their green camouflage on top, their toxin secretion that tastes awful, and their bobbing nasal calls.

name: Caecilian
teaser: The legless amphibian that looks like a worm

exploreAction.instruction: Read how caecilians are limbless burrowing amphibians found in tropical soil, looking like giant earthworms, with hidden eyes and sensory tentacles, some feeding their young with skin milk. Explore how they dig with reinforced skulls, their internal fertilization, and why they're the least known amphibian group.

name: Spadefoot Toad
teaser: The toad that digs with its feet

exploreAction.instruction: Read how spadefoot toads use sharp keratin spades on their hind feet to dig backwards into desert soil, emerging in explosive breeding frenzies after rare rains. Explore how tadpoles can metamorphose in just two weeks to beat drying pools, and how some species wait years between rains.

name: Clown Frog
teaser: The chubby leaf-dwelling frog of Borneo

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Bornean clown frog blends into fallen leaves with its dark blotched patterns, its oversized toe pads letting it perch on broad leaves. Explore its quiet life in peat swamps, its call, and how deforestation of Borneo threatens its leaf-litter habitat.

name: Newt
teaser: The salamander with the poison belly

exploreAction.instruction: Read how newts secrete potent toxins through their skin, with rough-skinned newts carrying tetrodotoxin, the same poison as pufferfish, and how garter snakes evolved resistance in a running arms race. Explore their aquatic spring breeding, their land-dwelling adult phase, and the toxic newt's bright belly.

name: Glass Frog
teaser: The frog with a see-through belly

exploreAction.instruction: Read how glass frogs of Central and South America have translucent belly skin that reveals their beating heart and organs, while their backs are leaf-green for camouflage. Explore why the transparency evolved, how males guard eggs over streams, and the threat of chytrid fungus.

name: Tadpole
teaser: The fish-like baby stage of frogs

exploreAction.instruction: Read how tadpoles are aquatic larval frogs that breathe through gills, graze on algae with tiny teeth, and undergo metamorphosis that rearranges their whole body into a frog. Explore the hormones driving the change, how some tadpoles eat meat or even siblings, and the fastest metamorphosis in desert pools.

name: Burrowing Frog
teaser: The frog that digs and inflates

exploreAction.instruction: Read how burrowing frogs dig backwards into soil with hardened feet, inflate their bodies to wedge themselves in burrows, and seal in moisture with a skin cocoon for months or years. Explore their explosive emergence after rain, their loud calls from underground, and how they store water.

name: Clownfish
teaser: The fish that lives inside a stinging anemone

exploreAction.instruction: Read how clownfish live among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones, protected by a mucus coat the anemone doesn't recognize, while they chase off anemone-eaters and bring it food. Explore the strict hierarchy in each anemone where the biggest fish is female, and how Nemo-style males can change sex.

name: Manta Ray
teaser: The gentle giant of the open ocean

exploreAction.instruction: Read how manta rays, with wingspans over 7 meters, glide through open oceans filter-feeding on plankton, sometimes leaping clear of the water. Explore their enormous brains for fish, their ability to recognize themselves in mirrors, and the cleaning stations where small fish groom them.

name: Archerfish
teaser: The fish that shoots water to hunt

exploreAction.instruction: Read how archerfish knock insects off overhanging branches by spitting jets of water, compensating for light refraction, and can even learn to knock down targets from meters away. Explore how they leap to catch falling prey, their accuracy that improves with practice, and their mangrove home.

name: Seahorse
teaser: The fish where the male gives birth

exploreAction.instruction: Read how male seahorses carry fertilized eggs in a brood pouch and give birth to hundreds of live young, the only animal where males undergo pregnancy. Explore how they swim upright, grip coral with prehensile tails, and how their monogamous courtship includes daily greetings.

name: Pufferfish
teaser: The fish that inflates into a spiky ball

exploreAction.instruction: Read how pufferfish gulp water to inflate into a spiky ball when threatened, while carrying tetrodotoxin, one of the most poisonous substances in nature. Explore why chefs train for years to serve fugu safely, and how these slow swimmers rely on defense over speed.

name: Great White Shark
teaser: The ocean's apex predator

exploreAction.instruction: Read how great white sharks grow to 6 meters, hunt with rows of serrated teeth that regrow constantly, and detect prey's heartbeat through electroreception. Explore their warm-blooded muscles for cold-water hunting, the mystery of breaching attacks, and how they learn by biting first.

name: Anglerfish
teaser: The deep-sea fish with a glowing lure

exploreAction.instruction: Read how female anglerfish lure prey in the dark deep sea with a glowing esca full of bioluminescent bacteria, and how tiny males bite onto females and fuse into permanent parasites. Explore the crushing pressures of their habitat, their enormous teeth, and the sheer weirdness of deep-sea life.

name: Electric Eel
teaser: The fish that zaps with 600 volts

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the electric eel of Amazon rivers generates up to 600 volts from three electric organs, using low-voltage pulses to sense prey and high-voltage bursts to stun it. Explore how they drive prey into a panic to force it out of hiding, and why they're not actually eels but knife fish.

name: Coelacanth
teaser: The fish thought extinct for 66 million years

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the coelacanth, thought to have gone extinct with the dinosaurs, was found alive off South Africa in 1938, unchanged for 400 million years. Explore its lobed fins that hint at the transition to land, its oily swim bladder, and how it gives birth to live young in deep caves.

name: Sailfish
teaser: The fastest fish in the ocean

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sailfish are clocked at speeds over 110 km/h, the fastest fish, using a tall retractable dorsal fin and a bill to slash through bait balls. Explore how they hunt in coordinated groups, taking turns to stun sardines, and their migrations across warm oceans.

name: Octopus
teaser: The eight-armed genius of the sea

exploreAction.instruction: Read how octopuses have three hearts, blue blood, nine brains, and can change color and texture in milliseconds, solve puzzles, use tools, and remember people. Explore how they squirt ink, regenerate arms, and the heartbreaking truth that females die after guarding eggs.

name: Cuttlefish
teaser: The master of disguise with 3D camouflage

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cuttlefish change color, pattern, and even texture, bumping skin into raised nubs to match their background in 3D, controlled by elastic pigment sacs and muscles. Explore their W-shaped pupils, their hypnosis of prey with pulsing waves, and their incredible camouflage intelligence.

name: Blobfish
teaser: The internet-famous deep-sea blob

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the blobfish, famous as the world's ugliest fish, looks normal in its natural habitat 1,000 meters deep where pressure holds its gelatinous body together, only sagging into the blob face when brought to the surface. Explore its low-energy life of floating and eating whatever drifts past.

name: Mudskipper
teaser: The fish that walks and climbs on land

exploreAction.instruction: Read how mudskippers of mangrove mudflats breathe air through their skin and the lining of their mouths, walk on leg-like fins, and even climb trees and rocks. Explore their burrows with air pockets, their territorial fights with raised fins, and how they keep their eyes moist.

name: Jellyfish
teaser: The drifting stinger that predates dinosaurs

exploreAction.instruction: Read how jellyfish, up to 95 percent water, drift through oceans using pulsing bells, their stinging tentacles firing microscopic harpoons, and how the immortal jellyfish can revert to its baby stage forever. Explore their blooms that clog beaches, and how they thrive where fish decline.

name: Barracuda
teaser: The silver missile with dagger teeth

exploreAction.instruction: Read how barracudas patrol reefs and open water with razor teeth, striking with explosive bursts of speed, sometimes following snorkelers out of curiosity. Explore their fearsome reputation vs reality, their habit of circling bait schools, and why their size can reach 2 meters.

name: Goblin Shark
teaser: The deep-sea shark with a slingshot jaw

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the goblin shark of the deep sea shoots its jaw forward like a slingshot to grab prey, a pink snout packed with electroreceptors for sensing prey in darkness. Explore how rarely humans see it, why it's called a living fossil, and how its flabby body suits crushing depths.

name: Bluefin Tuna
teaser: The warm-blooded speed machine of the sea

exploreAction.instruction: Read how bluefin tuna are warm-blooded fish that can sprint past 70 km/h and migrate across entire oceans, traveling thousands of kilometers to spawn. Explore their streamlined torpedo bodies, their ability to heat their muscles, and how overfishing drove them to the brink for sushi.

name: Flounder
teaser: The flatfish with both eyes on one side

exploreAction.instruction: Read how flounders start life swimming upright with eyes on both sides, then one eye migrates over the top of the skull as they settle onto the seafloor, both eyes ending on the same side. Explore how they change color to match the seabed and bury themselves in sand.

name: Lionfish
teaser: The beautiful invader with venomous spines

exploreAction.instruction: Read how lionfish, native to the Indo-Pacific with dramatic venomous spines, have invaded the Atlantic and Caribbean, eating native fish and breeding explosively with few natural predators. Explore the reef damage, the lionfish derbies and spearfishing to control them, and why their venom stings are rarely fatal.

name: Mandarinfish
teaser: The most colorful fish in the ocean

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the mandarinfish of Pacific reefs is drenched in electric blue, orange, and green, its color made by pigment cells rather than scales, and how it feeds on tiny crustaceans among coral rubble. Explore its dusk courtship dance where the pair rises together, and its mucus coat that protects it.

name: Arowana
teaser: The dragon fish that leaps for prey

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Asian arowana, called the dragon fish, leaps meters out of the water to catch insects, birds, and bats from overhanging branches, carrying eggs in its mouth to protect them. Explore why albino and gold varieties sell for six-figure prices, and why it's a symbol of luck in Asia.

name: Stonefish
teaser: The most venomous fish that hides as a rock

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the stonefish of Indo-Pacific reefs is the most venomous fish, camouflaged as an encrusted rock, delivering agonizing venom through dorsal spines that can kill within hours untreated. Explore the antidote, why divers must watch their step, and how its camouflage is nearly perfect.

name: Clown Knifefish
teaser: The fish that senses the world with electricity

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the clown knifefish of Southeast Asian rivers generates weak electric fields around its body to sense obstacles and prey in murky water, swimming with a rippling fin like a wave. Explore its knife-like body, how it hunts at night, and why it's prized by aquarists.

name: Parrotfish
teaser: The fish that poops sand

exploreAction.instruction: Read how parrotfish graze coral with beak-like fused teeth, crushing it to extract algae, and poop out fine sand, contributing to the white sand of tropical beaches. Explore their mucus sleeping cocoons, their color changes through life, and how some change sex from female to male.

name: Honeybee
teaser: The insect that runs the world's farms

exploreAction.instruction: Read how honeybees pollinate a third of the food we eat, dance to tell hive mates where flowers are, and live in colonies of tens of thousands ruled by a queen. Explore the waggle dance's coded directions, how bees make honey from nectar, and colony collapse threats.

name: Ants
teaser: The tiny farmers and soldiers of the soil

exploreAction.instruction: Read how ants outnumber humans by millions to one, with some farming fungus, herding aphids like cattle, and building bridges with their own bodies. Explore the queen's role, the division of labor by age, and leaf-cutter colonies of millions that outrank any single animal in biomass.

name: Monarch Butterfly
teaser: The butterfly that migrates 4,000 km

exploreAction.instruction: Read how monarch butterflies migrate up to 4,000 km to Mexican oyamel forests, with no single butterfly making the round trip, the great-grandchildren returning to the same trees. Explore how they navigate by the sun and magnetic field, the milkweed toxicity that protects them, and their spectacular roosts.

name: Dragonfly
teaser: The aerial predator with nearly 360 degree vision

exploreAction.instruction: Read how dragonflies intercept prey mid-flight with a brain that predicts where the target will be, controlling four independent wings and seeing nearly all around with compound eyes of up to 30,000 lenses. Explore their nymph stage underwater, their ancient 300-million-year history with 70 cm wingspans.

name: Ladybug
teaser: The gardener's little red ally

exploreAction.instruction: Read how ladybugs devour aphids, a single beetle eating thousands in its life, which is why gardeners love them, and why they flash red with spots, a warning of bitter defensive blood. Explore how they play dead, release yellow fluid from their knees, and huddle in hibernation masses.

name: Praying Mantis
teaser: The ambush predator with a swiveling head

exploreAction.instruction: Read how praying mantises wait motionless with folded raptorial arms, strike in 50 milliseconds, and swivel their heads nearly 180 degrees, the only insect that can look over its shoulder. Explore the famous and rare sexual cannibalism, their camouflage, and how they catch bees and even hummingbirds.

name: Firefly
teaser: The beetle that glows to find love

exploreAction.instruction: Read how fireflies produce cold light through bioluminescence to attract mates, each species flashing its own coded pattern, and some females mimic other species' flashes to lure and eat males. Explore the chemistry of luciferin, the glow of larvae called glowworms, and why light pollution dims their signals.

name: Stag Beetle
teaser: The beetle with antler-like jaws

exploreAction.instruction: Read how stag beetles duel with enormous mandibles shaped like deer antlers, males wrestling to win mates, while females' jaws are small and strong for chewing wood. Explore their six-year larval life chewing rotten wood, their size record in the insect world, and their decline as dead wood disappears.

name: Tarantula
teaser: The hairy giant that kicks venomous hairs

exploreAction.instruction: Read how tarantulas, despite their fearsome looks, mostly flee, flicking barbed urticating hairs at threats and only biting in defense with venom rarely dangerous to humans. Explore their molting to grow, their silk-lined burrows, and how females can live 30 years while males often die after mating.

name: Black Widow
teaser: The spider with the hourglass warning

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the black widow's red hourglass warns of a neurotoxic bite that causes severe muscle pain but is rarely fatal, with antivenom available. Explore its messy tangle web, the female's size and lifespan versus the male, and why its reputation exceeds its actual danger.

name: Jumping Spider
teaser: The spider with binocular vision

exploreAction.instruction: Read how jumping spiders have eight eyes including large forward-facing ones with binocular depth perception, stalking prey like tiny cats and leaping with a safety dragline. Explore their courtship dances, their ability to see color and even UV, and their unexpectedly sharp vision for creatures so small.

name: Scorpion
teaser: The armored stinger that glows under UV

exploreAction.instruction: Read how scorpions have survived for 400 million years, glowing blue-green under ultraviolet light, sensing vibrations through leg hairs, and some going a year without food. Explore their venom stings, how mothers carry young on their backs, and the pale desert species that hide by day.

name: Orb Weaver Spider
teaser: The spider that weaves a perfect wheel

exploreAction.instruction: Read how orb weavers spin circular webs in under an hour, engineering sticky spiral silk with a non-sticky radial skeleton, and rebuild daily. Explore how spider silk is stronger than steel by weight, how these spiders feel prey through web vibrations, and the classic garden web patterns.

name: Giant Trapdoor Spider
teaser: The ambush spider behind a hidden door

exploreAction.instruction: Read how trapdoor spiders dig burrows with hinged silk doors they hold shut, waiting under the lid to grab passing insects, and how females spend their whole lives in one burrow, living up to 40 years. Explore their armor, their docile reputation despite looks, and their ancient lineage.

name: Deathstalker Scorpion
teaser: The scorpion with the deadliest sting

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the deathstalker scorpion of North African deserts carries one of the most potent scorpion venoms, dangerous mainly to children and the elderly, while its venom yields molecules studied for brain cancer treatment. Explore its small size, its fluorescence under UV, and its burrow life.

name: Silk Moth
teaser: The moth that gave us silk

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the domesticated silkworm moth was bred over thousands of years for a single job, spinning a continuous silk cocoon thread up to a kilometer long that became the fabric of empires along the Silk Road. Explore how silk is unwound, why the moth can't fly, and the secret of its Chinese origin.

name: Cicada
teaser: The insect that waits 17 years underground

exploreAction.instruction: Read how periodical cicadas spend 13 or 17 years underground feeding on tree roots, then emerge by the billions in synchronized broods to sing, mate, and die in weeks. Explore why prime-number life cycles avoid predator cycles, their ear-splitting chorus, and the mystery of their timing.

name: Dung Beetle
teaser: The insect that navigates by the Milky Way

exploreAction.instruction: Read how dung beetles roll balls of dung far larger than themselves, navigate in straight lines using the Milky Way, the sun, or the moon, and some even climb on their ball to cool their feet. Explore their role in fertilizing soil and controlling flies, and their surprising strength.

name: Honey Pot Ant
teaser: The ant that becomes a living storage jar

exploreAction.instruction: Read how honey pot ants gorge on nectar until their abdomens swell into translucent amber orbs, hanging from nest ceilings as living food storage, regurgitating sweetness for the colony in lean times. Explore where Aboriginal people and desert peoples harvest these ants as sweet treats, and their underground nests.

name: Goliath Beetle
teaser: The heaviest insect on Earth

exploreAction.instruction: Read how goliath beetles of African rainforests weigh up to 100 grams, among the heaviest insects, with larvae that outweigh adults and shells so hard they're used as jewelry. Explore their swift flight, their sap and fruit diet, and their dramatic black and white patterns.

name: Atlas Moth
teaser: The moth with a 25 cm wingspan

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the atlas moth of Southeast Asia has a wingspan of 25 cm, among the largest moths, with wing tips shaped like snake heads to scare predators, and adults that don't eat, living only days on stored fat. Explore its silent flight, its female scent that attracts males from kilometers away, and its cocoon silk.

name: Bullet Ant
teaser: The ant with the most painful sting

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the bullet ant's sting is rated the most painful of any insect, a full day of throbbing agony, and how some Indigenous Amazonian boys endure it repeatedly as a rite of passage. Explore its large size, its colony defenses, and the neurotoxin that makes the sting unforgettable.

name: Butterfly Mimicry
teaser: The copycat strategy of butterfly wings

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the viceroy butterfly mimics the toxic monarch's orange and black pattern, a copycat strategy called Batesian mimicry that tricks predators into avoiding it, while the monarch's real toxicity is Mullerian, shared warning among distasteful species. Explore how predators learn to avoid the pattern, and how mimicry shaped evolution.

name: Termite
teaser: The architect of towering mud mounds

exploreAction.instruction: Read how termites build mounds up to 8 meters with internal ventilation that keeps the colony cool, farm fungus gardens, and digest wood through symbiotic microbes. Explore their queen that lays millions of eggs, their soldier castes, and how a single colony can contain millions.

name: Assassin Bug
teaser: The insect that liquifies prey

exploreAction.instruction: Read how assassin bugs stab prey with a dagger-like rostrum, inject digestive saliva, and suck out liquefied insides, with some species camouflaging themselves in the corpses of their prey. Explore the kissing bug's role in Chagas disease, their painful bites, and their patient ambush hunting.

name: Mantis Ootheca
teaser: The foamy egg case of the praying mantis

exploreAction.instruction: Read how praying mantises lay hundreds of eggs in a foamy ootheca that hardens into a protective case, overwintering until spring when dozens of tiny mantises hatch at once. Explore why the foam protects eggs from weather and parasites, and how the young disperse after their first molt.

name: Leafcutter Ant
teaser: The ant that farms fungus with leaf mulch

exploreAction.instruction: Read how leafcutter ants cut and carry leaf pieces up to 50 times their body weight back to underground gardens, not eating the leaves but feeding them to fungus they cultivate as their only food. Explore their mega-colonies of millions, their highway systems, and how their farming predates human agriculture by 50 million years.

name: Woolly Mammoth
teaser: The ice age giant we might bring back

exploreAction.instruction: Read how woolly mammoths roamed the frozen steppes with shaggy coats, humps of fat, and 5 meter tusks, preserved in permafrost so well that complete carcasses with fur and blood survive. Explore how they lived alongside humans who hunted and even drew them, and the science of trying to de-extinct them.

name: Sabre-toothed Cat
teaser: The ice age cat with 20 cm fangs

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sabre-toothed cats like Smilodon grew 20 cm canine teeth, too long to bite with, instead using powerful forelimbs to pin prey and slash the throat. Explore how their bites worked, why they vanished at the end of the ice age, and the famous La Brea tar pit fossils.

name: Dodo
teaser: The bird that became a symbol of extinction

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the dodo of Mauritius, a flightless pigeon weighing up to 20 kg, vanished within a century of humans arriving in 1598, from hunting and the pigs, rats, and monkeys sailors brought that ate its ground nests. Explore what we know from rare descriptions and bones, and why its story anchors conservation.

name: Dire Wolf
teaser: The giant wolf of the ice age

exploreAction.instruction: Read how dire wolves of the American ice age were bigger-boned than gray wolves, hunting horses, bison, and giant sloths in packs, and their fossils packed the La Brea tar pits. Explore what DNA reveals about them being a separate lineage, not a gray wolf ancestor, and why they died out with their prey.

name: Megalodon
teaser: The 18 meter shark that ruled the seas

exploreAction.instruction: Read how megalodon, an 18 meter shark three times the length of a great white, ruled warm oceans until a few million years ago, its teeth the size of a human hand found worldwide. Explore how scientists estimate its size and bite, why cooler seas and food loss likely killed it, and the myths of it surviving today.

name: Terror Bird
teaser: The flightless killer of South America

exploreAction.instruction: Read how terror birds were flightless predators up to 3 meters tall that ran down prey across South America, striking with huge hooked beaks before mammals became top predators. Explore how they dominated for 60 million years, the possible arms race with early mammals, and the mystery of their final extinction.

name: Quagga
teaser: The half-zebra that vanished in a century

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the quagga, a zebra relative with stripes only on its front, roamed South African plains in huge herds and was hunted to extinction by 1883, the last one dying in a zoo. Explore the famous photos, the quagga DNA that proves it a plains zebra subspecies, and the breeding project trying to bring its look back.

name: Great Auk
teaser: The northern penguin hunted to nothing

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the great auk, a flightless seabird of the North Atlantic that stood a meter tall and nested in huge colonies, was hunted for food, feathers, and specimens until the last two were killed in Iceland in 1844. Explore how its vulnerability on land doomed it, and its place as an extinction symbol.

name: Passenger Pigeon
teaser: The billions of birds that vanished

exploreAction.instruction: Read how passenger pigeons once darkened North American skies in flocks of billions, the most numerous bird on Earth, yet were hunted to extinction with the last bird, Martha, dying in 1914. Explore how their flocking made them easy targets, and how their loss still shapes forests and rewilding projects.

name: Thylacine
teaser: The Tasmanian tiger that might not be gone

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, a striped dog-like marsupial with a kangaroo pouch, was hunted to apparent extinction, the last known one dying in a zoo in 1936. Explore the unconfirmed sightings that keep hope alive, the recent DNA work on museum specimens, and attempts to resurrect it.

name: Ivory-billed Woodpecker
teaser: The ghost woodpecker of southern swamps

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the ivory-billed woodpecker, North America's largest, called the Lord God bird for the awe of its sighting, lost its swamp forests to logging and was declared extinct, though occasional unconfirmed sightings spark hope. Explore its dependence on old-growth dead trees, and the debates over whether it survives.

name: Baiji Dolphin
teaser: The river dolphin declared functionally extinct

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the baiji, a freshwater dolphin of China's Yangtze River with a legend of being a river goddess, was declared functionally extinct in 2007 after the river's shipping, fishing, and dams destroyed it. Explore what makes river dolphins so vulnerable, and why the baiji is a warning for other river species.

name: Moa
teaser: The giant flightless bird of New Zealand

exploreAction.instruction: Read how moas, New Zealand's flightless giants up to 3.6 meters tall, had no mammalian predators until Polynesian settlers arrived, hunting them and their giant eagle predator into extinction within a few centuries. Explore their ostrich-like size, their unique ecology, and the giant Haast's eagle that preyed on them.

name: Gigantopithecus
teaser: The biggest ape that ever lived

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Gigantopithecus, a giant ape of ancient Asia standing up to 3 meters tall and weighing 300 kg, is known only from teeth and jaws, yet was the largest primate ever. Explore why it likely died out when forests shrank, the bamboo diet theory, and how it inspired King Kong legends.

name: Woolly Rhinoceros
teaser: The ice age rhino with two horns

exploreAction.instruction: Read how woolly rhinos grazed ice age tundra with shaggy coats and a flattened horn for sweeping snow, their remains found frozen in permafrost and painted in cave art. Explore how they survived alongside mammoths, their diet of tough grasses, and the cave paintings of their encounters with early humans.

name: Cave Lion
teaser: The giant lion of the ice age

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cave lions, bigger than modern lions, prowled ice age Europe and Asia, leaving claw marks and bones in the caves they denned in, painted by early humans. Explore how DNA links them closer to modern lions than thought, their prey of deer and young mammoths, and why they vanished at the ice age's end.

name: Elephant Bird
teaser: The three meter bird of Madagascar

exploreAction.instruction: Read how elephant birds of Madagascar stood up to 3 meters and laid eggs with 9 liter capacity, the largest eggs of any animal, and were hunted to extinction by settlers. Explore how their huge eggs were used as water containers, their ostrich-like build, and what eggs and bones tell us about island life.

name: Giant Ground Sloth
teaser: The bear-sized slow giant of the Americas

exploreAction.instruction: Read how giant ground sloths, the size of elephants, shuffled across the Americas for millions of years, walking upright and maybe standing on hind legs to reach leaves. Explore how they survived ice ages, the debate over whether humans hunted them, and their ancient dung caves.

name: Animal Migration
teaser: The great journeys animals make each year

exploreAction.instruction: Read how animals migrate staggering distances, from wildebeest herds crossing crocodile-filled rivers to birds flying pole to pole, whales crossing oceans, and salmon returning to their birth streams. Explore how they navigate by stars, magnetic fields, and memory, and the dangers that make each journey a gamble.

name: Tool Use in Animals
teaser: The animals that use tools

exploreAction.instruction: Read how tool use spans the animal kingdom, from chimpanzees fishing termites with sticks and cracking nuts with stones, to crows bending wires into hooks, dolphins using sponges, and octopuses carrying coconut shells for shelter. Explore what tool use reveals about intelligence, and how it's learned and passed down.

name: Animal Mimicry
teaser: The art of looking like something else

exploreAction.instruction: Read how animals mimic everything, from harmless snakes copying venomous ones, to stick insects copying twigs, butterflies with eye patterns, and the amazing mimic octopus copying a dozen other sea creatures. Explore Batesian and Mullerian mimicry, how predators learn, and the arms race of deception.

name: Camouflage
teaser: The disappearing act of the animal world

exploreAction.instruction: Read how animals vanish into backgrounds through color, pattern, and texture, from snowshoe hares that turn white in winter to chameleons, flounders matching the seabed, and moths that look exactly like tree bark. Explore disruptive coloration, countershading, and how predators also use disguise to sneak up on prey.

name: Animal Communication
teaser: The languages of the wild

exploreAction.instruction: Read how animals communicate in astonishing ways, from whale songs that travel oceans to bee dances that describe flower locations, frog choruses, firefly flashes, and elephant infrasound rumblings felt through the ground. Explore how birds learn dialects, and what animal signals reveal about their inner lives.

name: Symbiosis
teaser: The partnerships that rule nature

exploreAction.instruction: Read how species partner in symbiosis, from clownfish and anemones, oxpeckers cleaning rhinos, cleaner wrasse fish servicing reef clients, to the fungi and algae inside lichens and the bacteria in our own guts. Explore mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism, and how these partnerships shaped life on Earth.

name: Hibernation
teaser: The long winter sleep

exploreAction.instruction: Read how animals survive winter by hibernating, dropping their body temperature and heart rate, from bears that don't eat for months to ground squirrels that cool to near freezing and marmots that wake to shiver every few weeks. Explore the difference from torpor, how fat is stored, and the science of suspended life.

name: Animal Intelligence
teaser: The clever minds of the wild

exploreAction.instruction: Read how intelligence appears across the animal kingdom, from crows that solve multi-step puzzles and remember human faces, to elephants that mourn, dolphins that recognize themselves in mirrors, pigs that play video games, and octopuses that open jars. Explore what animal minds reveal about how thought evolved.

name: Animal Courtship
teaser: The strangest dating rituals in nature

exploreAction.instruction: Read how animals court in spectacular ways, from bowerbirds building decorated love shacks, peacocks fanning iridescent trains, fireflies flashing coded signals, to birds of paradise dancing in costume-like plumage. Explore why females are picky, and how courtship drives some of nature's most extravagant features.

name: Animal Sleep
teaser: The strange sleeping habits of animals

exploreAction.instruction: Read how animals sleep in astonishing ways, from dolphins that rest one brain hemisphere at a time while swimming, swifts sleeping while flying, horses sleeping standing up, to bullfrogs that may not sleep at all. Explore why sleep matters, the trade-offs animals make, and the mystery of why we all need it.

name: Echolocation
teaser: Seeing with sound

exploreAction.instruction: Read how bats, dolphins, and some birds and shrews navigate and hunt by echolocation, sending out clicks and reading the echoes, with bats detecting a mosquito-sized target in complete darkness and dolphins seeing through murky water. Explore the biology of sound vision and how humans borrowed the idea for sonar.

name: Bioluminescence
teaser: The living light of the deep

exploreAction.instruction: Read how hundreds of species glow through bioluminescence, from fireflies signaling mates to deep-sea fish with glowing lures, anglerfish headlights, and glowing plankton that light up waves at night. Explore the chemistry of luciferin and luciferase, and the many uses of living light, from camouflage to communication.

name: Bird Migration Routes
teaser: The invisible highways of the sky

exploreAction.instruction: Read how billions of birds migrate along invisible flyways, from the Arctic tern's pole-to-pole marathon to geese flying in V-formations that save energy. Explore how birds fatten up, navigate by stars, sun, and magnetic sensing, and the stopover refueling spots whose loss can doom a species.

name: Social Insects
teaser: The superorganisms of the insect world

exploreAction.instruction: Read how ants, bees, termites, and wasps build societies that function like a single superorganism, with queens, workers, soldiers, and complex division of labor, from bee waggle dances to ant bridges and termite towers with air conditioning. Explore how simple individuals create collective intelligence.

name: Play in Animals
teaser: Why animals play

exploreAction.instruction: Read how animals play across species, from dogs and dolphins to crows, octopuses, and even spiders, practicing skills, testing social rules, and building bonds. Explore the theory that play is training for real life, how play signals differ from aggression, and why young animals play more.

name: Mimic Octopus
teaser: The octopus that imitates a dozen animals
byline: The shape shifter of the reef

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the mimic octopus of Southeast Asian reefs impersonates venomous and dangerous animals, flattening into a banded sea snake, spreading like a lionfish, or burying like a flounder, choosing the costume based on the threat. Explore how researchers discovered this, the limits of its mimicry, and why it stays near mud bottoms.

name: Do Animals Feel Emotions
teaser: The emotional lives of animals

exploreAction.instruction: Read how scientists now document grief in elephants that linger over the dead, joy in rats that laugh when tickled, jealousy in dogs, and comfort in chimpanzees that console friends after fights. Explore the evidence, the risks of anthropomorphism, and what brain and behavior studies reveal about animal feelings.

name: Monogamy in Animals
teaser: The pairs that stay together

exploreAction.instruction: Read how true lifelong monogamy is rare in nature, found in gibbons, albatrosses, prairie voles, and penguins, while many birds pair for a season then drift apart. Explore why monogamy evolves, the social bonds in prairie voles linked to oxytocin, and the DNA studies that find cheating even among faithful-looking pairs.

name: Animal Vision
teaser: How different animals see the world

exploreAction.instruction: Read how animals see the world very differently, from mantis shrimp with 12 color receptors to dogs with two, bees seeing ultraviolet flower patterns, snakes seeing heat, and eagles spotting prey kilometers away. Explore the physics and biology of eyes, and how each species' vision fits its life.

name: Whale Migration
teaser: The ocean's longest travelers

exploreAction.instruction: Read how gray whales swim 20,000 km round trips between Arctic feeding grounds and Mexican breeding lagoons, humpbacks sing through their migrations, and blue whales cross entire oceans. Explore how whales navigate, why they fast on the journey, and how researchers track them with tags.

name: Endangered Species
teaser: The species on the brink

exploreAction.instruction: Read how species go extinct at up to 1,000 times the natural rate, from rhinos poached for their horns and tigers losing forests to amphibians dying from a spreading fungus. Explore the Red List, the difference between endangered and critically endangered, and the rescue programs fighting to save species one by one.

name: Rewilding
teaser: Bringing wilderness back

exploreAction.instruction: Read how rewilding projects restore ecosystems by bringing back keystone species, from wolves returning to Yellowstone and reshaping rivers by controlling elk, to bison, lynx, and beavers returning across Europe. Explore the debate over what wild means, and how small reintroductions ripple through whole landscapes.

name: Poaching
teaser: The illegal hunt driving species to extinction

exploreAction.instruction: Read how poaching kills tens of thousands of elephants and rhinos for ivory and horn, pangolins for scales, and tigers for traditional medicine, funding criminal networks. Explore the demand that drives it, the rangers risking their lives, and how technology, tracking, and awareness are turning the tide.

name: Coral Reef Conservation
teaser: Saving the rainforests of the sea

exploreAction.instruction: Read how coral reefs shelter a quarter of all marine species but face warming that causes bleaching, with the Great Barrier Reef suffering repeated mass bleaching events. Explore reef restoration with coral nurseries, the fight against ocean acidification, and why protected marine parks give reefs their best chance.

name: Wildlife Corridors
teaser: The bridges that let animals roam

exploreAction.instruction: Read how highways and cities fragment habitats, and how wildlife corridors, from overpasses with trees and underpasses for bears and deer, reconnect wild populations, letting genes and animals flow. Explore famous examples like Banff's wildlife bridges, and how corridor design is now part of planning roads.

name: Captive Breeding
teaser: Saving species in zoos and labs

exploreAction.instruction: Read how captive breeding programs keep doomed species alive, from the California condor that dropped to 22 birds and came back through hand-raised chicks, to the Arabian oryx and black-footed ferret rescued from the brink. Explore the challenges of reintroducing animals raised in captivity, and the successes and failures.

name: Deforestation
teaser: The vanishing forests

exploreAction.instruction: Read how forests the size of football pitches are cleared every few seconds, driving orangutans, jaguars, and thousands of species toward extinction while releasing carbon. Explore the drivers from cattle and palm oil to logging, the difference between logging and clearing, and what sustainable choices can slow it.

name: Ocean Plastic
teaser: The plastic plague of the seas

exploreAction.instruction: Read how millions of tonnes of plastic enter oceans each year, entangling seals and turtles, filling albatross chicks' stomachs, and breaking into microplastics found in the deepest trenches and in seafood. Explore the garbage patches, the flow from rivers, and the global push for reduction and cleanups.

name: Animal Rescue
teaser: The teams saving animals from disaster

exploreAction.instruction: Read how rescue teams save animals from oil spills, floods, and poaching, from washing oiled penguins to rehabilitating orphaned elephants and releasing sea turtles with satellite tags. Explore the work of sanctuaries and clinics, the skill of caring for wild animals, and the releases that return survivors home.

name: Seed Banks
teaser: The vaults saving plant life

exploreAction.instruction: Read how seed banks freeze seeds from hundreds of thousands of plant species as insurance against extinction, from the Svalbard Global Seed Vault carved into Arctic permafrost to national banks worldwide. Explore how seeds are dried and frozen, why crop diversity matters for food security, and how banks help restore damaged landscapes.

name: CITES
teaser: The treaty that protects endangered trade

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species, CITES, regulates the global trade in wildlife, from ivory and rhino horn to orchids and parrots, with member countries agreeing to ban or restrict what crosses borders. Explore its three appendices, the fight against smuggling, and the loopholes smugglers exploit.

name: Marine Protected Areas
teaser: The ocean parks that heal the sea

exploreAction.instruction: Read how marine protected areas let overfished oceans recover, with no-take zones where fish grow larger and reefs rebound, from the Great Barrier Reef's zones to the Galapagos reserve. Explore how protected areas help beyond their borders through spillover, and the global goal of protecting 30 percent of oceans by 2030.

name: Conservation Technology
teaser: The gadgets saving wildlife

exploreAction.instruction: Read how technology now fights extinction, from drones counting nests and thermal cameras catching poachers, to DNA analysis of ivory tracing smuggling networks, camera traps catching snow leopards, and AI identifying whale calls. Explore how cheap sensors and satellites give conservationists eyes across the wild.

name: Great Ape Conservation
teaser: Saving our closest relatives

exploreAction.instruction: Read how orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, and bonobos all face habitat loss, poaching, and disease, with mountain gorillas surviving a scare to under 1,000 individuals before patient protection doubled them. Explore the rangers, vets, and communities behind the comebacks, and what great ape survival means for forests.

name: Rainforest Alliance
teaser: The label that protects forests and farmers

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Rainforest Alliance certification labels coffee, chocolate, tea, and bananas grown with standards that protect forests, wildlife, and worker rights, working with small farms across the tropics. Explore how the frog seal began in 1987, the audit system, and how consumer choices can shift whole industries.

name: Wetlands
teaser: The marshes that filter and flood-control

exploreAction.instruction: Read how wetlands, from mangroves to marshes and peat bogs, filter pollution, store floodwater, and shelter birds, yet over half the world's wetlands have been drained. Explore the Ramsar Convention protecting them, the carbon locked in peat, and how restored wetlands can shield coasts from storms.

name: Blue Whale
teaser: The largest animal that ever lived

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the blue whale is the largest animal ever, up to 33 meters and 190 tonnes, bigger than any dinosaur, with a heart the size of a car and a tongue that weighs as much as an elephant. Explore how it filter-feeds on krill, sings subsonic songs, and how whaling nearly erased it before protection.

name: African Elephant
teaser: The gentle giant with the amazing trunk

exploreAction.instruction: Read how African elephants, the largest land animals, use their trunks of 40,000 muscles for everything from breathing to picking up a single peanut, and their huge ears radiate heat. Explore their matriarchal herds, their memory, their grief for the dead, and the ivory trade's threat.

name: Giraffe
teaser: The tallest animal on Earth

exploreAction.instruction: Read how giraffes reach 5.5 meters on necks of just seven vertebrae, each 25 cm long, with a heart that pumps blood up two meters against gravity using pressure valves in the neck. Explore their blue-black prehensile tongues, their dangerous necking fights, and how they sleep only minutes a day.

name: Cheetah
teaser: The sprinter of the savanna

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cheetahs accelerate from zero to 100 km/h in three seconds, the fastest land animal, with non-retractable claws for grip, a flexible spine, and a tail used as a rudder. Explore why they hunt by day, their high failure rate, and how cubs lose to lions and hyenas despite adult speed.

name: Gorilla
teaser: The gentle giant of the forest

exploreAction.instruction: Read how gorillas, our closest relatives after chimpanzees, live in family troops led by silverback males that can be 10 times stronger than a human, yet are gentle vegetarians. Explore their knuckle walking, their nests built fresh each night, their sign language abilities, and the fight to save mountain gorillas.

name: Polar Bear
teaser: The largest land predator

exploreAction.instruction: Read how polar bears, the largest land carnivores weighing up to 700 kg, hunt seals from sea ice, with black skin under translucent fur and paw pads that grip ice. Explore their incredible swimming, their dependence on shrinking sea ice, and why they're the symbol of climate change.

name: Kangaroo
teaser: The pouched jumper of Australia

exploreAction.instruction: Read how red kangaroos hop at up to 60 km/h using elastic tendons that store energy, cover 8 meters in a bound, and can't walk backwards. Explore the pouch where tiny jelly-bean sized joeys develop, their boxing fights, and how they survive drought by pausing embryo development.

name: Koala
teaser: The marsupial that eats poison

exploreAction.instruction: Read how koalas survive almost entirely on eucalyptus leaves that are toxic to most animals, thanks to a long gut and special microbes, and sleep up to 20 hours a day because the leaves are poor fuel. Explore the difference between koalas and bears, the joey's pouch life, and chlamydia's threat.

name: Lion
teaser: The king with a social kingdom

exploreAction.instruction: Read how lions are the only cats that live in prides, cooperative groups of related females who hunt together while males defend the territory. Explore the lion's roar heard 8 km away, why males grow manes, the cubs' communal care, and the harsh reality of life and death on the savanna.

name: Tiger
teaser: The largest cat with the orange stripes

exploreAction.instruction: Read how tigers, the largest cats reaching 300 kg, have striped skin under striped fur, no two patterns alike, and stalk alone through Asian forests. Explore their night vision, their swimming ability unlike other cats, and how poaching and habitat loss pushed them to a few thousand in the wild.

name: Otter
teaser: The playful river and sea acrobat

exploreAction.instruction: Read how otters are built for water, with webbed feet, dense fur that traps air, and the ability to hold breath for minutes, some sea otters floating on their backs cracking clams with stones. Explore their playful slides and games, their tool use, and how river otters raise pups in hidden dens.

name: Orangutan
teaser: The red ape of the treetops

exploreAction.instruction: Read how orangutans, the only great apes of Asia, live almost entirely in trees, building fresh nests nightly, using leaves as umbrellas and tools, and teaching their young for up to a decade. Explore their name meaning person of the forest, their intelligence, and the palm oil crisis destroying Borneo's forests.

name: Hippopotamus
teaser: The river giant that kills more than lions

exploreAction.instruction: Read how hippos, weighing up to 3 tonnes, spend days submerged with just eyes and nostrils out, their skin secreting a red sunscreen, and gallop surprisingly fast on land. Explore why they're among Africa's most dangerous animals, how they breathe underwater, and their vital role fertilizing rivers with dung.

name: Rhinoceros
teaser: The armored giant with a horn of keratin

exploreAction.instruction: Read how rhinos, weighing up to 2.5 tonnes, have horns made of compressed keratin like fingernails, thick skin like armor, and poor eyesight but sharp hearing and smell. Explore the five rhino species, the poaching crisis for their horns worth more than gold, and the armed guards protecting the last northern whites.

name: Platypus
teaser: The egg-laying mammal with a duck bill

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the platypus is a mammal that lays eggs, has a duck-like bill that detects electricity, a beaver-like tail, webbed feet, and venomous spurs on males' ankles. Explore why it confused early scientists, how it hunts blind underwater with electroreception, and its monotreme relatives.

name: Chimpanzee
teaser: Our closest living relative

exploreAction.instruction: Read how chimpanzees share about 98 percent of our DNA, use sticks to fish termites, crack nuts with stones, hunt monkeys in coordinated packs, and have distinct cultures passed between communities. Explore their politics, their capacity for empathy and war, and why Jane Goodall's work changed how we see them.

name: Wolf
teaser: The ancestor of every dog

exploreAction.instruction: Read how gray wolves hunt in structured packs with a complex social order, communicate through howls that carry 10 km, and once roamed most of the northern hemisphere.
