Explore their role as keystone predators, how Yellowstone's wolves reshaped the ecosystem, and how every dog descends from them.

name: Dolphin
teaser: The smiling genius of the sea

exploreAction.instruction: Read how bottlenose dolphins use echolocation to see through murky water, call each other by individual names, form lifelong alliances, and teach hunting tricks to their young. Explore their intelligence, their playful surfing and leaping, and how they sleep with half a brain awake.

name: Sloth
teaser: The slowest mammal on Earth

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sloths move so slowly that algae grows in their fur, camouflaging them and providing nutrients, and they descend from trees only once a week to poop. Explore their upside-down life, their three-toed claws, their slow metabolism, and how slowness is an energy-saving survival strategy.

name: Armadillo
teaser: The mammal in armor

exploreAction.instruction: Read how armadillos wear flexible bony armor, the three-banded one rolling into a perfect ball, and they dig burrows, can hold their breath underwater for minutes, and some species give birth to identical quadruplets. Explore their insect diet, their cousins, and their Texas expansion.

name: Giant Anteater
teaser: The mammal with the 60 cm tongue

exploreAction.instruction: Read how giant anteaters lick up to 30,000 ants and termites a day with a 60 cm tongue that whips in and out 150 times a minute, and fend off jaguars with razor-sharp front claws. Explore their strong smell, their shaggy tails used as blankets, and their solitary wanderings.

name: Bat
teaser: The only mammal that truly flies

exploreAction.instruction: Read how bats are the only mammals that fly, with wings of skin stretched over elongated fingers, and most navigate by echolocation, emitting up to 200 calls a second. Explore their huge diversity, a quarter of all mammals, their roles eating insects and pollinating plants, and how they host but rarely spread viruses.

name: Beaver
teaser: The engineer that reshapes rivers

exploreAction.instruction: Read how beavers build dams and lodges that create wetlands, their orange teeth never stop growing, and they fell trees with chisel teeth and store branches underwater for winter. Explore how beaver ponds boost biodiversity, the near-extinction from fur trapping, and the rewilding projects bringing them back.

name: Meerkat
teaser: The standing sentry of the desert

exploreAction.instruction: Read how meerkats live in mobs of up to 40 in the Kalahari, taking turns as sentries standing on hind legs to watch for eagles, while others dig for insects and babysit pups. Explore their teaching of pups to hunt scorpions, their war with rival mobs, and their tough desert life.

name: Narwhal
teaser: The unicorn of the sea

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the narwhal's tusk is actually a spiraled tooth up to 3 meters long, a sensory organ packed with nerves, found mostly on males, and once traded as unicorn horns. Explore how narwhals live in Arctic waters, dive past 1,500 meters, and how the tusk's role is still debated.

name: Pangolin
teaser: The scaled mammal that rolls into a ball

exploreAction.instruction: Read how pangolins are the only mammals covered in scales, rolling into an armored ball so tight even lions give up, and using a 40 cm tongue to eat ants and termites. Explore how they're the most trafficked animal in the world for their scales, and the rescue and anti-trafficking fight.

name: Snow Leopard
teaser: The ghost of the mountains

exploreAction.instruction: Read how snow leopards of the Himalayas leap 15 meters between cliffs, wrap their tails around themselves like scarves, and are so elusive locals call them ghosts. Explore their thick spotted fur, their bluish-grey eyes, their shrinking habitat, and the camera-trap studies trying to count them.

name: Wombat
teaser: The marsupial that poops cubes

exploreAction.instruction: Read how wombats produce cube-shaped droppings, the only animal known to do so, stacking them to mark territory, and their backward-facing pouches protect joeys while digging. Explore their powerful burrows, their armor-like rear ends used to block attackers, and their surprisingly fast sprint.

name: Red Panda
teaser: The firefox that's not a panda

exploreAction.instruction: Read how red pandas of Himalayan bamboo forests are not closely related to giant pandas, more like raccoons and weasels, using a false thumb to grip bamboo and a tail with ring patterns for balance. Explore their bamboo-heavy diet, their shy tree life, and how they gave the Firefox browser its name.

name: Walrus
teaser: The tusked giant of the Arctic ice

exploreAction.instruction: Read how walruses use their long tusks to haul their 1.5 tonne bodies onto ice, defend against polar bears, and rake the seabed for clams, vacuuming them up with powerful lips. Explore their whiskers that sense prey, their massive haul-out gatherings, and the shrinking sea ice that threatens them.

name: Gibbon
teaser: The singing acrobat of the treetops

exploreAction.instruction: Read how gibbons swing through trees with arm-swinging brachiation at speeds that would break human shoulders, and sing duets with mates that echo through the forest, some pairs harmonizing perfectly. Explore their small ape size, their monogamy, and why they're called lesser apes.

name: Capybara
teaser: The world's largest rodent

exploreAction.instruction: Read how capybaras, the largest rodents at up to 66 kg, live in groups by rivers in South America, half-submerged with eyes, ears, and nostrils on top of their heads, and are famous for their calm, social nature that seems to make every animal their friend. Explore their swimming, their teeth, and their giant family groups.

name: Fossa
teaser: Madagascar's top predator

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the fossa of Madagascar is the island's largest predator, a cat-like mongoose relative that hunts lemurs through the trees with semi-retractable claws and a tail for balance. Explore why Madagascar evolved such unique predators, the fossa's endangered status, and its secretive life.

name: Echidna
teaser: The spiny egg-laying mammal

exploreAction.instruction: Read how echidnas are monotremes that lay eggs, then carry the puggle in a pouch, covered in spines with a long snout for lapping ants and termites, and males have a four-headed penis used in rotation. Explore their brain structure shared with the platypus, and their odd breeding behavior.

name: Spotted Hyena
teaser: The misunderstood hunter with the female leader

exploreAction.instruction: Read how spotted hyenas are powerful hunters, not just scavengers, with clans ruled by dominant females larger than males, and their famous laugh is a call of submission or excitement. Explore their bone-crushing jaws, their cubs that fight from birth, and their matriarchal society.

name: Jaguar
teaser: The spotted cat that crushes skulls

exploreAction.instruction: Read how jaguars of the Americas have the strongest bite of any big cat, piercing skulls with their canines, and unlike other big cats they love water, swimming and hunting caiman and fish. Explore their rosette spots, their solitary territories, and their role as rainforest guardians.

name: Manatee
teaser: The gentle sea cow

exploreAction.instruction: Read how manatees, or sea cows, graze seagrass in warm coastal waters, weighing up to 600 kg yet moving gently, and must surface to breathe every few minutes. Explore their huge slow metabolism, their mermaid myth, and how boat strikes threaten them.

name: Lemur
teaser: The monkey-like primate of Madagascar

exploreAction.instruction: Read how lemurs exist only in Madagascar, evolving in isolation into over 100 species from tiny mouse lemurs to the howling indri, with ring-tailed lemurs sunbathing in troops and stink-fighting with their tails. Explore why Madagascar is a primate ark, and the deforestation endangering every species.

name: Ant-eating Mammals
teaser: The animals that eat ants and termites

exploreAction.instruction: Read how ant and termite specialists evolved separately in different continents, from the giant anteater and tamandua of the Americas, the pangolin of Africa and Asia, and the aardvark of Africa, each developing long sticky tongues and powerful digging claws. Explore convergent evolution at work.

name: Seal
teaser: The ocean acrobat that comes ashore

exploreAction.instruction: Read how seals are marine mammals that dive for fish, some like the elephant seal diving 1,500 meters for up to two hours, sleeping underwater, and coming ashore to breed and molt. Explore the difference between true seals and sea lions, their whiskers that sense fish wakes, and their clumsy-yet-graceful double life.

name: Silverback Gorilla
teaser: The day of a silverback

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a silverback gorilla leads his troop through the forest, deciding when to feed, rest, and travel, breaking up squabbles, and protecting his family from threats, even dying to defend them. Explore how his silver hair signals maturity, his huge strength, and how Dian Fossey's studies revealed his gentle leadership.

name: Tarsier
teaser: The primate with enormous eyes

exploreAction.instruction: Read how tarsiers of Southeast Asia have eyes bigger than their brains, each eye the size of their whole eyeball, letting them hunt insects in darkness, and can rotate their heads almost 360 degrees. Explore their leaping between trees, their high-pitched calls, and why they're fragile in captivity.

name: Musk Ox
teaser: The shaggy survivor of the ice age

exploreAction.instruction: Read how musk oxen survived the ice age, forming a defensive circle around calves against wolves, with underwool called qiviut softer than cashmere and warmer than wool. Explore their Arctic life, their massive curved horns used in head-on clashes, and their reintroduction to Alaska.

name: Dugong
teaser: The seagrass grazer that inspired mermaids

exploreAction.instruction: Read how dugongs of the Indian Ocean and Australia graze seagrass meadows, the only strictly marine herbivorous mammal, slow and gentle, and are thought to have inspired sailors' mermaid tales. Explore their migrations, their breathing every few minutes, and how seagrass loss and nets threaten them.

name: Cheetah Cubs
teaser: The dangerous first year of a cheetah cub

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cheetah cubs face a brutal first year, with up to 90 percent killed by lions, hyenas, and starvation while their mother hunts alone, and a mother may raise one in ten cubs to adulthood. Explore the mohawk of fur that helps camouflage them, their cub-sitting dens, and the sanctuary programs protecting orphan cubs.

name: Honey Badger
teaser: The fearless badger that fights lions

exploreAction.instruction: Read how honey badgers of Africa and Asia are legendary for fearlessness, attacking snakes, stinging bee hives, and even fighting off lions and hyenas, with thick loose skin that lets them twist and bite back. Explore their intelligence, their tool use, and their name from a mutual bird partnership.

name: Okapi
teaser: The forest giraffe with zebra legs

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the okapi of Congo rainforests looks like a mix of giraffe and zebra, the giraffe's only living relative, with a long blue tongue that cleans its ears and a striped rear for camouflage. Explore how it was unknown to science until 1901, its secretive life, and the war and poaching threats in Congo.

name: Caribou
teaser: The deer that migrates in vast herds

exploreAction.instruction: Read how caribou of the Arctic tundra make some of the longest land migrations, herds of hundreds of thousands moving over 5,000 km a year, with hooves that change with the seasons for snow and muskeg. Explore how both sexes grow antlers, the wolves that follow them, and the decline of herds.

name: Axolotl as a Pet
teaser: The beginner's guide to keeping an axolotl

exploreAction.instruction: Read how axolotls make fascinating pets that stay aquatic and young-looking their whole lives, but need cool water below 20 degrees, no gravel they might swallow, and a protein-rich diet of worms and pellets. Explore why they're illegal in some places, their 15 year lifespan in captivity, and the joy of watching them regenerate.

name: Betta Fish Care
teaser: Keeping the Siamese fighting fish happy

exploreAction.instruction: Read how betta fish, famous for their flowing fins and aggression toward each other, thrive in warm, planted tanks with gentle filters, not tiny bowls, eating high-protein pellets and frozen foods. Explore why males fight, the bubble nests males build, and how to keep them healthy for years.

name: Dog Domestication
teaser: How wolves became man's best friend

exploreAction.instruction: Read how dogs were domesticated from gray wolves at least 15,000 years ago, likely when wolves scavenged camps and self-selected for tameness, and how breeding created everything from chihuahuas to Great Danes. Explore the Siberian fox experiment, the genes for friendliness, and the ancient burials showing dogs as family.

name: Cat Domestication
teaser: The cat that domesticated itself

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cats likely domesticated themselves, drawn to grain stores and the mice they attracted, with the earliest evidence in the Near East 10,000 years ago, and they remain genetically close to wildcats. Explore how cats were worshipped in Egypt, sailed the world on ships, and became the internet's favorite animal.

name: Animal World Records
teaser: The biggest, fastest, and strangest in nature

exploreAction.instruction: Read how nature's records stagger, from the blue whale as the largest animal ever and the peregrine falcon as the fastest, to the immortal jellyfish that cheats death, the loudest animal being the pistol shrimp's sonic snap, and the longest-lived being Greenland sharks passing 400 years. Explore what each record reveals about adaptation.

name: Fastest Animals
teaser: The speed champions of land, sea, and sky

exploreAction.instruction: Read how speed records are set across the animal kingdom, from the peregrine falcon stooping at 300 km/h and the cheetah sprinting to 100 km/h on land, to sailfish at 110 km/h in water and dragonflies accelerating harder than fighter jets. Explore the physics of their bodies, and how speed trades off with endurance.

name: Strongest Animals
teaser: The strongest lifters in nature

exploreAction.instruction: Read how strength scales wildly, with the dung beetle pulling over 1,100 times its body weight, leafcutter ants carrying 50 times theirs, and elephants moving fallen trees, while the blue whale's sheer power dwarfs all. Explore why small animals seem strongest relative to size, and the physics of scaling.

name: Longest-lived Animals
teaser: The animals that outlive everyone

exploreAction.instruction: Read how some animals live for centuries, with Greenland sharks passing 400 years, bowhead whales over 200, giant tortoises over 150, and the ocean quahog clam documented at 500, while the hydra may be effectively immortal. Explore the biology of aging, telomeres, and what their longevity teaches us.

name: Giant Squid
teaser: The deep-sea monster finally filmed alive

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the giant squid, a legend of the deep for centuries with arms reaching 13 meters and eyes the size of dinner plates, was only filmed alive in its natural habitat in 2012 after decades of searching. Explore its battles with sperm whales, its suckers ringed with teeth, and what we still don't know about it.

name: Colossal Squid
teaser: The heaviest invertebrate with swiveling hooks

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the colossal squid of Antarctic waters is heavier than the giant squid, up to 500 kg, with swiveling hooks on its tentacles and eyes the size of basketballs, the largest eyes in the animal kingdom. Explore the few specimens ever recovered, including the frozen 8 meter female in New Zealand, and its battles with sperm whales.

name: Vampire Squid
teaser: The deep-sea creature that's neither vampire nor squid

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the vampire squid of deep oxygen-poor waters is neither vampire nor squid but its own order, with a cloak-like web between its arms it wraps around itself, and eyes the largest relative to body size of any animal. Explore how it survives on marine snow in the oxygen minimum zone, and why its name is a myth.

name: Coconut Octopus
teaser: The octopus that carries its own shelter

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the coconut octopus of tropical seas is one of the few invertebrates known to use tools, carrying coconut shells and clam halves, walking on two arms like a stilt walker, and assembling them into a portable shelter. Explore the studies that filmed this behavior, and what it says about octopus intelligence.

name: Blue-ringed Octopus
teaser: The tiny octopus with deadly venom

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the blue-ringed octopus, small enough to fit in a palm, carries tetrodotoxin in its bite that can paralyze a human within minutes, with no antivenom, while flashing brilliant blue rings as a warning. Explore how its venom is made by symbiotic bacteria, its shy nature, and why the flash means back off.

name: Nautilus
teaser: The living fossil in a spiral shell

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the chambered nautilus has drifted in spiral shells for 500 million years, barely changed, using chambers to control buoyancy, and jetting backward for propulsion. Explore how it lives at depth by day and rises to feed at night, its pinhole eyes without lenses, and the pearl-like shell trade that threatens it.

name: Squid
teaser: The fast jets of the ocean

exploreAction.instruction: Read how squid are torpedo-shaped cephalopods that jet backward by blasting water through a funnel, changing color with pigment cells, and some species flash and school in coordinated shoals. Explore their three hearts, their ink defense, their fast growth, and the giant squid's deep-sea cousins.

name: Hermit Crab
teaser: The crab that lives in borrowed shells

exploreAction.instruction: Read how hermit crabs have soft unprotected abdomens and must find empty snail shells to live in, swapping as they grow and lining up in queues to trade shells, sometimes fighting for a good one. Explore their shell-changing rituals, the sea anemones they carry for protection, and how plastic litter tricks them into deadly shell homes.

name: Peacock Mantis Shrimp
teaser: The crustacean with a punch like a bullet

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the peacock mantis shrimp delivers the fastest punch in the animal kingdom, a club strike that accelerates like a bullet, cavitates water and can smash aquarium glass, with eyes carrying 12 color receptors and independent movement. Explore its smasher versus spearer forms, and why its punch breaks shells and crab armor.

name: Lobster
teaser: The armored scavenger of the seafloor

exploreAction.instruction: Read how lobsters grow throughout life by molting, can live past 50 years, and use one crushing claw and one cutting claw, flipping backward to escape, and some believe they don't age biologically. Explore their underwater migration lines, their role as bottom scavengers, and the debate over boiling them alive.

name: Crab
teaser: The sideways walker of shores and seas

exploreAction.instruction: Read how crabs walk sideways on jointed legs, their first pair modified into claws, and thousands of species live from deep sea to desert, with some like the coconut crab climbing trees and others like spider crabs wearing camouflage. Explore their molting, their soft-shell stage, and their ancient armored body plan.

name: Pistol Shrimp
teaser: The shrimp with a sonic snap

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the pistol shrimp snaps a giant claw so fast it creates a collapsing bubble that produces a shockwave hotter than the sun's surface and a sound louder than a gunshot, stunning or killing prey. Explore the sonoluminescence of the snap, the flash of light it makes, and how snapping shrimp colonies hum through the sea.

name: Krill
teaser: The tiny shrimp that feeds the ocean

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Antarctic krill, shrimplike crustaceans just 6 cm long, swarm in billions and form the foundation of the Antarctic food web, eaten by whales, seals, penguins, and fish. Explore their daily vertical migrations, their glowing swarms, the fishing industry harvesting them, and how climate change affects their sea-ice nursery.

name: Barnacle
teaser: The crustacean that stands on its head

exploreAction.instruction: Read how barnacles are crustaceans, related to crabs, that glue themselves to rocks, ship hulls, and even whales, standing on their heads and kicking food into their mouths with feathery legs. Explore their cement that's studied for surgical glue, their penis that can stretch many times their body length, and how they choose settlement spots.

name: Coconut Crab
teaser: The largest land-living arthropod

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the coconut crab of Pacific islands is the largest land arthropod, up to 4 kg with a leg span of a meter, climbing trees and cracking coconuts with its powerful claws. Explore its return-to-sea breeding, its scavenging diet that once included Amelia Earhart theories, and how islands' giant crabs evolved from hermit crabs.

name: Woodlouse
teaser: The isopod that lives under rocks

exploreAction.instruction: Read how woodlice are crustaceans, the only ones fully adapted to land, breathing through gill-like pleopods and needing damp places, some curling into balls and others like the giant isopod growing 30 cm in the deep sea. Explore their role as recyclers, their unusual urine that smells, and their sudden sea-living relatives.

name: Sea Star
teaser: The five-armed predator that regrows
byline: The star of the tide pool

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sea stars are echinoderms with tube feet that grip, a stomach they push outside to digest prey, and the superpower of regrowing lost arms, with some species splitting in half to reproduce. Explore the crown-of-thorns that devastates coral, and why they're not fish.

name: Sea Urchin
teaser: The spiny ball of the seafloor

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sea urchins move on tube feet among spines, graze algae with a five-toothed jaw called Aristotle's lantern, and can devastate kelp forests when their predators vanish. Explore the purple urchin explosion along Pacific coasts, their roe prized as uni sushi, and their role in reef ecosystems.

name: Sea Cucumber
teaser: The squishy vacuum of the seafloor

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sea cucumbers crawl across the seafloor vacuuming sediment for food, defend by ejecting sticky organs or their own guts to distract predators, and some breathe through their rear ends. Explore their role recycling ocean nutrients, the alarming trade in them for Asian cuisine, and their farming in marine ponds.

name: Brittle Star
teaser: The starfish that runs on arms

exploreAction.instruction: Read how brittle stars, more slender than sea stars, move rapidly by wriggling their five arms, some species living in the thousands on a single coral head, and they detach arms to escape predators, regrowing them. Explore their deep-sea dominance, their light-sensing arms, and the difference from true sea stars.

name: Sand Dollar
teaser: The flattened sea urchin of sandy shores

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sand dollars are flattened sea urchins that burrow in sandy seabeds, using tiny spines to move and tube feet to pass food to their mouths, their five-petaled patterns are breathing pores. Explore how they feed on sand grains, the keyhole sand dollar's slits, and why beachcombers love their skeletons.

name: Crinoid
teaser: The feather star of the deep

exploreAction.instruction: Read how crinoids, or feather stars and sea lilies, are ancient echinoderms that have drifted for 500 million years, arms waving to catch plankton, some anchored on stalks like lilies and others free-swimming. Explore their fossil abundance in limestone, their filtering arms, and their comeback in modern reefs and deep sea.

name: Sea Anemone
teaser: The flower that stings

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sea anemones look like flowers but are predators, stinging with tentacles packed with harpoon-like nematocysts, and can live for decades or centuries, some splitting in half to clone themselves. Explore their partnership with clownfish, their slow gliding over rocks, and their relatives, corals and jellyfish.

name: Coral
teaser: The animal that builds reefs

exploreAction.instruction: Read how corals are colonies of tiny animals called polyps that build limestone skeletons, the reefs they create housing a quarter of all marine species, and they feed at night with stinging tentacles while getting most energy from algae in their tissues. Explore how bleaching happens when warming seas expel those algae, and the race to save reefs.

name: Portuguese Man o' War
teaser: The floating colony that's not a jellyfish

exploreAction.targetName: Meet the Portuguese man o' war
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Portuguese man o' war is not a jellyfish but a siphonophore, a colony of specialized animals working as one, with a gas-filled float, stinging tentacles that can trail 30 meters, and venom that can hospitalize swimmers. Explore its wind-driven sailing, the beaches it washes onto, and the painful stings it leaves.

name: Box Jellyfish
teaser: The most venomous animal in the sea

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Australian box jellyfish is considered the most venomous animal, its tentacles carrying enough toxin to kill an adult within minutes, with a more advanced nervous system and 24 eyes, some with lenses, that let it steer toward prey. Explore the vinegar first-aid, the nets and stinger suits, and its surprising swimming ability.

name: Immortal Jellyfish
teaser: The jellyfish that cheats death

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Turritopsis dohrnii, the immortal jellyfish, can revert from its adult stage back to a polyp when stressed, restarting its life cycle and potentially living forever, the only animal known to do this. Explore how the process works, whether it truly avoids death, and what it teaches about aging and regeneration.

name: Comb Jelly
teaser: The glowing paddle drifter

exploreAction.instruction: Read how comb jellies are not true jellyfish but ctenophores, moving with eight rows of shimmering comb-like paddles that scatter rainbow light, and many glow, with some species cannibalistic and one that fuses with others when injured. Explore their place near the base of the animal tree, and their sticky colloblast cells instead of stings.

name: Sponge
teaser: The animal that filters the sea

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sea sponges are animals despite lacking brains, muscles, or organs, pumping seawater through their bodies to filter food, some species with skeletons of glass needles and others harvested for bathing. Explore how they can regrow from single cells, their chemical defenses that inspire drugs, and their ancient 600-million-year history.

name: Glass Sponge
teaser: The sponge that builds with glass

exploreAction.instruction: Read how glass sponges of the deep sea build skeletons of silica spicules so intricate they've inspired optical fiber design, and some reefs of these sponges off Canada are over 9,000 years old, the oldest living animal communities. Explore how they trap plankton with their glass lattices, and the trawling that destroys them.

name: Venus Flower Basket
teaser: The sponge that hosts a shrimp pair

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Venus flower basket is a glass sponge that traps a pair of tiny shrimp inside, which live their whole lives there, breeding until they die together, giving it a wedding symbolism in Japanese culture. Explore how its glass lattice inspired architects, and the delicate deep-sea habitat it needs.

name: Snail
teaser: The shelled slow mover

exploreAction.instruction: Read how snails glide on a single muscular foot with slime, retreat into spiral shells, and use a rasping radula tongue with thousands of microscopic teeth, with some species like the cone snail hunting fish with venom harpoons. Explore the giant African land snail, the garden snail's homing, and how snails helped map human brain cells.

name: Cone Snail
teaser: The beautiful shell with a harpoon bite

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cone snails hunt with a harpoon-like tooth loaded with conotoxin venom, so potent and precise that some species can kill a human, while the venom's peptides are studied as medicines for pain. Explore the geography cone's deadly reputation, the fish-hunting strategy, and why collectors handle shells with gloves.

name: Oyster
teaser: The bivalve that filters and makes pearls

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a single oyster filters up to 100 liters of water a day, cleaning estuaries, while some oysters coat irritants in nacre to form pearls, and reefs of them once formed natural barriers. Explore oyster farming, the difference between natural and cultured pearls, and restoration projects rebuilding oyster beds.

name: Giant Clam
teaser: The clam with a living garden

exploreAction.instruction: Read how giant clams of Indo-Pacific reefs grow over a meter long and 200 kg, hosting algae in their colorful mantles that feed them sugars while they filter feed, growing reef structure. Explore their strong shell muscle, the overharvesting that shrank populations, and their role in reef ecology.

name: Octopus Arms
teaser: The nine brains of the octopus

exploreAction.instruction: Read how each octopus arm has its own mini-brain with hundreds of millions of neurons, so arms can taste, feel, and act semi-independently, with a central brain issuing goals while arms solve the details. Explore the studies of arm autonomy, how octopuses control eight flexible limbs, and what it reveals about distributed intelligence.

name: Nudibranch
teaser: The sea slug with stolen weapons

exploreAction.instruction: Read how nudibranchs, flamboyant sea slugs, steal stinging cells from the anemones and jellyfish they eat and deploy them in their own gills, while their bright colors warn predators. Explore their other chemical defenses, their short dramatic lives, and why divers call them jewels of the reef.

name: Chiton
teaser: The mollusc with a shell of armor plates

exploreAction.instruction: Read how chitons wear a shell of eight overlapping plates that let them curl into a ball, clinging to rocks in crashing waves with a foot of immense grip, and some have eyes made of mineral aragonite embedded in their shells. Explore the gumboot chiton's red underside, their radula with metal-hard teeth, and their ancient lineage.

name: Cuttlefish Camouflage
teaser: How cuttlefish vanish in a blink

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cuttlefish change color and texture in under a second by expanding and contracting pigment sacs and muscles that raise skin nubs, matching not just color but the 3D texture of their background. Explore the studies on their camouflage decisions, their colorblind eyes that somehow sense color, and the limits of their disguise.

name: Sea Snail
teaser: The shells of the shore

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sea snails graze shores and reefs with radula teeth, many in spiraled shells, from the tiny periwinkle to the giant whelk that drills into clams with acid and a rasping tongue. Explore how shells grow, the spiral geometry of their homes, and the roles they play from tide pool to deep sea.

name: Whelk
teaser: The drilling predator of the shore

exploreAction.instruction: Read how whelks are predatory sea snails that drill holes through clam and mussel shells with their radula and acid, then inject digestive fluids and suck out the meal. Explore their egg capsules called sea washballs, their cannibalistic habits, and their role controlling shellfish populations.

name: Mussel
teaser: The bivalve that grips with threads

exploreAction.instruction: Read how mussels anchor to rocks with byssal threads, a protein glue so tough it's studied for underwater adhesives, and filter plankton while cleaning the water. Explore the freshwater mussels whose larvae hitch rides on fish gills, the invasive zebra mussel problem, and mussel farming as sustainable food.

name: Radula
teaser: The toothed tongue of molluscs

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the radula, a ribbon of thousands of microscopic teeth found in most molluscs, works like a conveyor-belt rasp, used by snails to scrape algae, cone snails to harpoon fish, and chitons to grind rock with teeth reinforced with iron. Explore the variety of radula designs and how each fits its owner's diet.

name: Horseshoe Crab
teaser: The blue-blooded living fossil

exploreAction.instruction: Read how horseshoe crabs have survived over 450 million years with blue copper-based blood that clots on contact with bacteria, the basis of the Limulus amebocyte lysate test used to check every injectable medicine for contamination. Explore their role as shorebird food, the bleeding and return program, and the synthetic alternatives in development.

name: Feather Duster Worm
teaser: The worm that blooms like a flower

exploreAction.instruction: Read how feather duster worms live in leathery tubes and extend crowns of feathery tentacles to filter plankton, retreating instantly into their tubes when disturbed. Explore how they regenerate lost crowns, their reef and aquarium lives, and the difference between worms that look like flowers and the flowers that look like nothing else.

name: Bobbit Worm
teaser: The ambush worm with scissor jaws

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the bobbit worm, up to 3 meters long, buries itself in reef sand and strikes passing fish with five jaws that snap shut like scissors, dragging prey into its burrow. Explore its iridescent body, the aquariums it terrorized by eating fish overnight, and how little we know of its deep-sea cousins.

name: Velvet Worm
teaser: The caterpillar-like hunter with glue guns

exploreAction.instruction: Read how velvet worms are ancient invertebrates that spray prey with quick-hardening glue from slime glands, then chew with their jaws, and have changed little in 400 million years. Explore their water-dwelling ancestors, their live birth, their velvet-soft skin, and why they link arthropods and worms in evolutionary history.

name: Tardigrade
teaser: The microscopic survivor that outlives everything

exploreAction.instruction: Read how tardigrades, or water bears, microscopic eight-legged animals, survive boiling, freezing, vacuum of space, radiation, and decades without water by drying into a tun state and reviving when wet. Explore where they live from moss to deep sea, their DNA-copying heat-shock proteins, and what makes them nearly indestructible.

name: Earthworm
teaser: The humble soil engineer

exploreAction.instruction: Read how earthworms tunnel through soil, aerating it and recycling organic matter into fertile castings, with a single acre of healthy soil holding up to a million worms. Explore their five hearts, their regeneration, how they sense light, and Charles Darwin's lifelong study of their importance.

name: Giant African Land Snail
teaser: The giant snail that eats everything

exploreAction.targetName: Meet the giant African land snail
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the giant African land snail grows to 20 cm and 1 kg, eats hundreds of plant species, lays hundreds of eggs, and spreads diseases, making it one of the world's worst invasive species, repeatedly intercepted at ports. Explore how it arrived in Florida and was eradicated twice, and its dual life as pest and food.

name: Rotifer
teaser: The microscopic animal that comes back from the dead

exploreAction.instruction: Read how rotifers are microscopic aquatic animals with ciliated crowns that look like spinning wheels, and bdelloid rotifers can survive freezing, drying, and radiation for years, reviving with DNA repair, and have reproduced without sex for millions of years. Explore their ability to survive in the Antarctic permafrost for decades.

name: Anemonefish Partnership
teaser: The deal between fish and anemone

exploreAction.instruction: Read how anemonefish, or clownfish, live safely among stinging anemone tentacles by building up a protective mucus coat the anemone doesn't recognize, while chasing off anemone-eating fish and providing nutrients with their waste. Explore the research on how they acquire immunity, their strict size hierarchy, and what happens when the anemone dies.

name: Amoeba
teaser: The shape-shifting single cell

exploreAction.instruction: Read how amoebas are single-celled protists that move and eat by flowing pseudopods, engulfing food by phagocytosis, and some, like the brain-eating Naegleria, are famous for the wrong reasons. Explore their reproduction by simple division, the giant deep-sea xenophyophores that grow to 10 cm, and why they're not animals or plants.

name: Planarian
teaser: The flatworm that regenerates a new body

exploreAction.instruction: Read how planarians can regrow an entire body from a fragment of 1/279th of themselves, thanks to powerful stem cells called neoblasts, and even regrow heads with functional brains, storing memories across regeneration in some experiments. Explore their light-sensitive eyespots, their flat ribbon bodies, and their role in regeneration research.

name: Echidna Spines
teaser: Why the echidna wears a coat of spikes

exploreAction.instruction: Read how echidnas defend with up to 5,000 modified hairs that are sharp spines, rolling into a spiky ball or digging into the ground leaving only spikes exposed, and males use spines in mating rivalry. Explore how spines grow from fur follicles, the difference from hedgehog quills, and the echidna's prehistoric spiky relatives.

name: Hammerhead Shark
teaser: The shark with a hammer-shaped head

exploreAction.instruction: Read how hammerhead sharks use their wide hammer-shaped heads to improve electroreception and vision, swinging their heads like metal detectors to scan the seafloor for rays, and some species school in the hundreds. Explore why the head evolved, their deep dives, and the fin trade's threat to them.

name: Whale Shark
teaser: The gentle filter-feeding giant

exploreAction.instruction: Read how whale sharks, the largest fish at over 18 meters, filter-feed on plankton and tiny fish with a mouth a meter wide, each individual wearing a unique spot pattern like a fingerprint. Explore their migration to feeding aggregations, their long life and late maturity, and the tourism that can protect them.

name: Great White Hunting Strategy
teaser: How great whites hunt seals

exploreAction.instruction: Read how great white sharks hunt seals by launching from below at high speed, sometimes breaching fully out of the water, using the seal's dark silhouette against the surface to target it, and biting first to investigate. Explore the elephant seal colonies that draw them, and the reasons attacks on humans are often mistaken identity.

name: Basking Shark
teaser: The second largest fish that eats plankton

exploreAction.instruction: Read how basking sharks, second only to whale sharks, cruise with mouths open wide enough to swallow a person, straining plankton through gill rakers, and migrate thousands of kilometers following blooms. Explore why they're rarely seen, the mystery of where they winter, and their vulnerability to ships and nets.

name: Nurse Shark
teaser: The sleepy bottom dweller of the reefs

exploreAction.instruction: Read how nurse sharks rest in piles on reef bottoms, sucking prey from crevices with their mouths, and are docile but have a powerful bite if provoked. Explore their night feeding, their names from the sucking sound they make, and how they give birth to live young.

name: Megalodon vs Great White
teaser: The giant ancient shark compared to today's

exploreAction.instruction: Read how megalodon, extinct for 3.6 million years, reached three times the length of today's great white, with teeth over 15 cm, while great whites share its ocean but not its size or bite force. Explore how scientists compare them through teeth and vertebrae, and what megalodon's extinction left behind.

name: Tiger Shark
teaser: The garbage can of the sea

exploreAction.instruction: Read how tiger sharks eat almost anything, from sea turtles and birds to license plates and tires, earning the nickname garbage can of the sea, with striped juveniles that fade with age. Explore their role as top predator, their huge litters, and the notorious attacks that gave them a bad name.

name: Reef Sharks
teaser: The patrol of the coral reef

exploreAction.instruction: Read how blacktip, whitetip, and grey reef sharks patrol coral reefs, keeping fish populations healthy, and their presence is a sign of reef health. Explore the shark feeding frenzies when fishing boats arrive, their daytime resting caves, and how overfishing empties reefs of their sharks.

name: Leopard Seal
teaser: The apex predator of the Antarctic ice

exploreAction.instruction: Read how leopard seals, the only seals that hunt warm-blooded prey, ambush penguins at the water's edge with immense jaws, and also filter krill with specialized teeth, while curious encounters with divers reveal a complex personality. Explore their solitary life, their vocal underwater songs, and their feared yet fascinating role in Antarctica.

name: Orca
teaser: The killer whale that hunts in family pods

exploreAction.instruction: Read how orcas, the largest dolphins, hunt in matrilineal family pods with distinct dialects and cultures, some specializing in fish, others in seals, whales, or even sharks, coordinating ambushes that rival wolf packs. Explore their intelligence, their black and white pattern, and why no orca has ever killed a human in the wild.

name: Humpback Whale Song
teaser: The haunting songs of the humpback

exploreAction.instruction: Read how humpback whales sing complex songs that evolve over years, with all males in a population singing the same version, and populations far apart even sharing new verses. Explore why they sing, the song's structure from phrases to themes, and how hydrophones reveal whales carrying songs across oceans.

name: Beluga
teaser: The canary of the sea

exploreAction.instruction: Read how belugas, the white whales of the Arctic, are called canaries of the sea for their whistles and clicks, have flexible necks that let them nod, and use echolocation under sea ice to find breathing holes. Explore their molting in estuaries, their social pods, and how their Arctic home is warming.

name: Sperm Whale
teaser: The deep diver with the biggest brain

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sperm whales dive over 2,000 meters for up to 90 minutes hunting squid, carrying the largest brain on Earth and a head full of spermaceti oil that helps with buoyancy and echolocation. Explore the matriarchal pods, the scars from giant squid battles, and how their clan dialects vary like human cultures.

name: Dolphin Echolocation
teaser: The sonar of the sea

exploreAction.instruction: Read how dolphins send out focused clicks that bounce off objects, building detailed sound pictures that reveal fish density, seabed shape, and even a target's internal structure, with some species like the Amazon river dolphin navigating floodplains by sound alone. Explore the melon that focuses clicks, the jaw that receives echoes, and how sonar engineers borrowed the design.

name: Seal Whiskers
teaser: The underwater sensing whiskers of seals

exploreAction.instruction: Read how seals and sea lions use whiskers called vibrissae to detect water movements, allowing a blindfolded seal to follow a fish's wake minutes after it passed, and how some can sense the pressure trail of a submarine. Explore the whisker follicle structure, the physics of wake tracking, and how the design inspires underwater robots.

name: Walrus Tusks
teaser: The multi-purpose tusks of the walrus

exploreAction.instruction: Read how walrus tusks are elongated canine teeth that grow throughout life, used for hauling onto ice, fighting, and signaling status, while walruses actually feed by vacuuming clams from the seabed with their lips, not the tusks. Explore the size difference between males and females, the tusks' sensory nerves, and the myths about tusk use.

name: Seagrass Grazers
teaser: The dugong and manatee meadows

exploreAction.instruction: Read how dugongs and manatees graze seagrass meadows like underwater cows, with dugongs feeding in long furrows that stimulate regrowth, and their grazing maintaining healthy seagrass for fish nurseries. Explore the seagrass ecosystems that store carbon, the threats from boats and pollution, and the protected zones that shelter the grazers.

name: Lion vs Tiger
teaser: The kings of the savanna and the jungle

exploreAction.instruction: Read how lions and tigers, the two largest cats, split from a common ancestor under a million years ago, tigers being solitary and larger with stripes, lions social and maned, and the two never meet in the wild but have been pitted against each other in history. Explore their size records, their different hunting styles, and the hybrids bred in captivity.

name: Leopard
teaser: The strong climber of the big cats

exploreAction.instruction: Read how leopards are the most widespread big cat, hauling prey heavier than themselves into trees to keep it from lions and hyenas, with spots called rosettes and near-night vision. Explore their adaptability from rainforest to city edge, their stealth, and the melanistic black panther form.

name: Cougar
teaser: The big cat of the Americas

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cougars, also called mountain lions and pumas, hold records for the most names of any animal, roam the Americas from Canada to Patagonia, and leap 6 meters from a standstill. Explore their solitary territories, their ambush hunting of deer, and their remarkable comeback in populated regions.

name: Clouded Leopard
teaser: The big cat with the longest fangs

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the clouded leopard of Southeast Asian forests has the longest canine teeth relative to body size of any cat, almost sabre-like, and is the most ancient lineage of big cats, an expert climber that can hang upside down from branches. Explore its cloud-patterned coat, its near-vertical tree climbing, and the forests disappearing beneath it.

name: Caracal
teaser: The tufted-eared jumper of the savanna

exploreAction.instruction: Read how caracals leap nearly 3 meters straight up to knock birds out of the air, with black ear tufts and a face like a lynx, and their name comes from a Turkish word for black ears. Explore their savanna and desert life, their springing hunts, and their history of being tamed for hunting in ancient cultures.

name: Ocelot
teaser: The spotted cat of the Americas

exploreAction.instruction: Read how ocelots, once hunted for their beautiful spotted coats, are small wild cats of the Americas that hunt on the forest floor at night, their fur pattern making them nearly invisible in dappled light. Explore their river-edge territories, their status symbol past, and their quiet recovery where protected.

name: Lynx
teaser: The snowshoe cat of northern forests

exploreAction.instruction: Read how lynx are adapted for snow with huge furry paws that act like snowshoes, ear tufts that may aid hearing, and a diet almost entirely of snowshoe hares, so hare cycles drive lynx numbers. Explore the Eurasian lynx's return to Europe, the Canada lynx of the boreal forest, and the bobcat, its southern cousin.

name: Serval
teaser: The long-legged hunter of the grassland

exploreAction.instruction: Read how servals have the longest legs relative to body size of any cat, leaping 3 meters into the air to catch birds, and using huge ears to hear rodents underground before pouncing. Explore their grassland home in Africa, their near 60 percent hunting success, one of the highest of cats, and their spotted coats.

name: Cheetah vs Leopard
teaser: Telling the two spotted cats apart

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cheetahs and leopards, both spotted African cats, differ in build, spots, and lifestyle, cheetahs slim and built for speed with solid black spots and tear marks, leopards stocky with rosette spots and no tear marks, and the two rarely interact since cheetahs hunt by day and leopards by night. Explore the easy field guide to telling them apart.

name: Snow Leopard Cubs
teaser: Raising cubs on the roof of the world

exploreAction.instruction: Read how snow leopard mothers raise cubs in remote mountain dens, nursing them for months, teaching them to stalk through steep terrain, and keeping them hidden for their first year while defending territory that can span 1,000 square kilometers. Explore the cubs' smoky coats, their stay with mothers into their second year, and the camera traps that finally documented dens.

name: Bengal Tiger
teaser: The national animal of India

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Bengal tigers, the most numerous tiger subspecies, roam Indian forests and mangroves, with the Sundarbans population famous for swimming between islands and a reputation built on rare but feared attacks. Explore their stripes unique as fingerprints, their territorial roaring, and the reserves like Ranthambhore that protect them.

name: Siberian Tiger
teaser: The largest cat in the world

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Siberian or Amur tigers are the largest cats, males reaching 300 kg, surviving in the snowy forests of Russia's Far East with thick fur and fat, hunting wild boar and deer across huge territories. Explore their comeback from near extinction under strict protection, and the corridors needed to connect their scattered populations.

name: The Lioness Hunt
teaser: How lionesses hunt as a team

exploreAction.instruction: Read how lionesses do most of the hunting in a pride, coordinating flanking maneuvers, with one driving prey toward hidden others, and only succeeding in about a quarter of hunts. Explore the teamwork against buffalo and wildebeest, the male's role eating first, and how cubs learn hunting skills through play.

name: Nile Crocodile
teaser: Africa's largest reptile

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Nile crocodiles grow to 5 meters, ambush wildebeest and zebra at river crossings, and have survived unchanged for millions of years, with a reputation earned from real attacks on people. Explore their nesting mounds, their temperature-dependent sex determination, and the crocodile-watching spots where crossings are pure drama.

name: Snake Senses
teaser: How snakes see the world without ears

exploreAction.instruction: Read how snakes sense the world through flicking tongues that carry scent molecules to a vomeronasal organ, some with heat-sensing pits that see infrared, jaw bones that hear ground vibrations, and some like sea snakes with vision sharpened underwater. Explore the combination of senses that makes them such precise hunters in darkness.

name: Venomous Snakes
teaser: The world's deadliest snakes

exploreAction.instruction: Read how venomous snakes use venom for hunting and defense, from neurotoxins of cobras and mambas to the hemotoxins of vipers, with the inland taipan carrying the most toxic venom drop for drop while the saw-scaled viper likely kills the most people. Explore how antivenom is made, and why most snakes bite humans only in self-defense.

name: Python Hunting
teaser: How constrictors kill without venom

exploreAction.instruction: Read how pythons and boas kill by constriction, coiling around prey and tightening with each exhale until the heart and blood flow fail, then swallowing prey whole with jaws that unhinge and stretch. Explore how they sense warm prey, how big their meals can get, and the record Burmese pythons swallowing deer in Florida.

name: Gecko Calls
teaser: The geckos that talk

exploreAction.instruction: Read how some geckos are among the most vocal lizards, the tokay gecko named for its loud tokay call that echoes through tropical nights, with males calling to claim territory and attract mates, and some species defending territory with chirps. Explore the different calls, why geckos are named after their sounds, and the nocturnal chorus of Southeast Asian walls.

name: Desert Lizards
teaser: How lizards survive the world's harshest heat

exploreAction.instruction: Read how desert lizards survive extreme heat by burrowing, shifting activity to dawn and dusk, standing on two legs or raising their bodies off hot sand, and some like the thorny devil collecting water through skin channels. Explore the fringe-toed lizard that dives into sand dunes, and the shingleback's slow desert life.

name: Sea Snake
teaser: The most venomous snakes of the ocean

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sea snakes are among the most venomous snakes, fully adapted to ocean life with paddle tails, the ability to absorb oxygen through skin, and the capacity to dive deep and hold breath for hours. Explore why they rarely bite humans, their live birth at sea, and the myths surrounding their venom.

name: American Alligator
teaser: The comeback king of the swamps

exploreAction.instruction: Read how American alligators, once hunted to the edge of extinction, rebounded to millions across the Southeast, living up to 50 years, growing to 4.5 meters, and building mounds that shelter many other species. Explore their cold-blooded basking, their gator holes that keep wetlands alive in drought, and the difference from crocodiles.

name: Frilled-neck Lizard vs Basilisk
teaser: The two famous lizards compared

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Australia's frilled lizard scares predators with a neck frill and runs on two legs, while Central America's basilisk runs across water, both famous for dramatic escapes. Explore how each evolved its own extreme, the frill's display role, and the water-running trick of the basilisk's wide-fringed toes.

name: Komodo Dragon Senses
teaser: The smelling, sensing giant lizard

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Komodo dragons detect carrion from 10 km away using a forked tongue and vomeronasal organ, flicking scents out of the air, and their vision and hearing are sharp enough to track prey, with venom glands studied only in 2009. Explore the taste buds in their throats, their tongue-flicking behavior, and how they locate wounded prey over days.

name: Slow Worm
teaser: The legless lizard mistaken for a snake

exploreAction.instruction: Read how slow worms are legless lizards, not snakes, with eyelids, ear openings, and the ability to shed their tails, and they live in gardens and grasslands eating slugs and snails. Explore why they're gardeners' friends, their blue-spotted males, and how to tell them from snakes.

name: Garter Snake
teaser: The harmless backyard snake

exploreAction.instruction: Read how garter snakes are among the most common and harmless snakes of North America, eating slugs, worms, and frogs, gathering in huge mating balls each spring, and some even give birth to live young. Explore their range across Canada and the US, their mild musk defense, and why they're great neighbors.

name: Box Turtle
teaser: The land turtle with a hinged shell

exploreAction.instruction: Read how box turtles carry a hinged shell that closes completely, sealing them into an armored box, and can live 50 to 100 years, wandering home ranges they know intimately. Explore their omnivorous appetite, their need for large wild areas, and why pet trade and roads threaten them.

name: Crocodilian Family
teaser: The three branches of armored reptiles

exploreAction.instruction: Read how crocodilians split into three families, true crocodiles with narrow snouts, alligators and caimans with broad snouts, and the gharial with its long thin snout, all sharing ancient ancestry with dinosaurs. Explore how snout shape fits diet, the salt glands of crocodiles that alligators lack, and the fossil giants like Sarcosuchus that dwarfed modern forms.

name: Green Iguana
teaser: The tree-dwelling giant of the Americas

exploreAction.instruction: Read how green iguanas grow to 1.8 meters, basking in treetops and dropping into water with a splash when threatened, with a third eye on their forehead that senses light and shadows. Explore their mostly leaf diet, their territorial displays, and their spread as pets gone wild in Florida.

name: Chameleon Tongue
teaser: The fastest tongue in the animal kingdom

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a chameleon's tongue can shoot out at 26 body lengths per second, longer than its whole body, powered by elastic collagen and a ring of accelerator muscles, with a sticky pad that grabs insects and reels them in. Explore the physics of the projection, the mucus grip, and how high-speed cameras revealed the mechanism.

name: Tasmanian Devil
teaser: The feisty scavenger of Tasmania

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Tasmanian devils, the largest carnivorous marsupials, scavenge with bone-crushing jaws and unleash ear-splitting screams and snarls, with a contagious face cancer that nearly wiped them out. Explore their pouch babies, their island home, and the breeding programs and vaccine research fighting devil facial tumor disease.

name: Quokka
teaser: The smiling marsupial of Rottnest

exploreAction.instruction: Read how quokkas, small wallaby-like marsupials of Rottnest Island, Australia, became internet famous for their apparent smiles, which are actually a feature of their muzzle, not a mood. Explore their plant diet, their fearlessness around people that made selfies possible, and why tourists flock to see them.

name: Opossum
teaser: The North American marsupial that plays dead

exploreAction.instruction: Read how opossums, North America's only marsupials, play dead so convincingly that they enter a catatonic state with hanging tongue and foul smell, and are master survivors eating ticks, garbage, and anything else. Explore their prehensile tails, their 13 nipples, and why they're immune to most snake venom.

name: Bilby
teaser: The Easter bunny of Australia

exploreAction.instruction: Read how bilbies, rabbit-eared marsupials of the Australian desert, dig spiral burrows that shelter other species and are threatened by foxes, cats, and fire, with conservation groups selling chocolate bilbies at Easter to replace the bunny. Explore their long snouts, their nocturnal life, and the captive breeding and fence programs saving them.

name: Bandicoot
teaser: The cone-digging marsupial

exploreAction.instruction: Read how bandicoots dig characteristic cone-shaped holes in gardens and bushland hunting insects and fungi, with a pouched marsupial body and a diet that spreads fungal spores vital to forests. Explore their rapid reproduction, their vulnerable status from foxes and cats, and how their digging aerates soil.

name: Numbat
teaser: The termite-eating striped marsupial

exploreAction.instruction: Read how numbats are termite specialists with no pouch, carrying young on their backs, and can eat 20,000 termites a day using a long sticky tongue, their striped backs making them look like small tigers. Explore their decline from foxes, the reintroduction programs with guard dogs and fenced reserves, and their diurnal hunting unlike most marsupials.

name: Cuscus
teaser: The slow-climbing possum of New Guinea

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cuscuses are slow-climbing possums of New Guinea and neighboring islands, with thick fur, grasping tails, and a vegetarian diet of leaves and fruit, some species with striking white or spotted coats. Explore their night activity, their role in island ecosystems, and the hunting and habitat loss threatening them.

name: Wallaby
teaser: The smaller cousin of the kangaroo

exploreAction.instruction: Read how wallabies are kangaroo relatives found across Australia, from the rock wallabies that leap between cliffs with gripping soles to the swamp wallabies of forests, all hopping with the same elastic tendons as kangaroos. Explore their many species, their pouch life, and their roles from mountains to coasts.

name: Mole
teaser: The underground excavator with star hands

exploreAction.instruction: Read how moles dig tunnels with oversized shovel-like front paws, swimming through soil at speed, and the star-nosed mole finds prey with 22 fleshy tentacles in under a quarter second, the fastest eater in the animal kingdom. Explore their poor eyesight, their earthworm larders, and how their tunneling aerates the soil.

name: Shrew
teaser: The tiny mammal with a fierce appetite

exploreAction.instruction: Read how shrews have the highest metabolism of any mammal, eating up to three times their body weight daily, and some like the water shrew and short-tailed shrew carry venom in their saliva. Explore their constant eating, their heart rates over 1,000 beats a minute, and how they survive winter by shrinking their own skulls and organs.

name: Hedgehog
teaser: The spiky night wanderer of gardens

exploreAction.instruction: Read how hedgehogs are covered in up to 5,000 hollow spines, roll into a ball to sleep and defend, and snuffle through gardens at night eating insects, with a skill for climbing and even swimming. Explore their hibernation, their decline from traffic and gardens without holes, and how to help them.

name: Flying Squirrel
teaser: The squirrel that glides between trees

exploreAction.instruction: Read how flying squirrels glide up to 90 meters using furry membranes stretched between wrists and ankles, steering with their tails, and they're nocturnal, unlike daytime tree squirrels. Explore the physics of their gliding, their nests in tree hollows, and the Japanese giant flying squirrel the size of a cat.

name: Prairie Dog
teaser: The town builder of the plains

exploreAction.instruction: Read how prairie dogs build vast underground towns with separate chambers for nurseries and bathrooms, and have one of the most sophisticated animal alarm systems, with different calls for different predators. Explore their role as keystone species feeding ferrets, eagles, and badgers, and the ranching conflicts over their grazing.

name: Jerboa
teaser: The kangaroo-hopping desert rodent

exploreAction.instruction: Read how jerboas of Asian and African deserts hop on elongated hind legs like tiny kangaroos, covering 3 meters a leap, and can survive without drinking, getting water from seeds. Explore their huge ears that radiate heat, their burrow life avoiding the heat of day, and their extraordinary leaps to escape predators.

name: Naked Mole Rat
teaser: The wrinkly rodent that feels no pain

exploreAction.instruction: Read how naked mole rats live in eusocial colonies like bees, with a queen and workers, tolerate near-zero oxygen and high carbon dioxide, feel almost no pain, resist cancer, and can live over 30 years, far longer than other rodents. Explore their underground African life, their cold-blooded temperature regulation, and what they teach us about aging.

name: Binturong
teaser: The bear cat that smells like popcorn

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the binturong, or bearcat, of Southeast Asian forests smells like buttered popcorn, a scent from a chemical in its urine, and is neither bear nor cat but a viverrid related to civets. Explore its prehensile tail used like a fifth hand, its slow tree-climbing life, and its threatened forest home.

name: Kinkajou
teaser: The honey bear of the rainforest

exploreAction.instruction: Read how kinkajous, called honey bears, of Central and South American rainforests use 40 cm tongues to lick nectar and honey, living in trees with prehensile tails, and are related to raccoons, not bears. Explore their night activity, their social fruit-feeding groups, and their vocal repertoire from barks to screams.

name: Okapi Discovery
teaser: The mystery animal found in 1901

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the okapi was one of the last large mammals discovered, its existence rumored by locals as the African unicorn until 1901, when a specimen reached London and stunned science, proving a forest-dwelling giraffe relative with zebra legs. Explore how it stayed hidden so long in Congo's Ituri rainforest, and what else might still hide there.

name: Springbok
teaser: The leaping antelope of southern Africa

exploreAction.instruction: Read how springboks leap up to 3.5 meters in stiff-legged jumps called pronking, displaying a crest of white hair, and historically gathered in herds of millions that streamed across the veld. Explore their drought survival on desert shrubs, their speed, and the mass migrations that once rivaled the Serengeti.

name: Saiga Antelope
teaser: The antelope with the strange nose

exploreAction.instruction: Read how saiga antelopes of Central Asian steppes wear huge inflatable noses that filter dust and warm cold air, and their mass migrations once numbered millions, crashing to tens of thousands from hunting and disease. Explore the mass die-offs that puzzled scientists, the nasal cooling system, and the fences that block their ancient routes.

name: Axolotl Regeneration
teaser: How axolotls regrow anything

exploreAction.instruction: Read how axolotls regrow complete limbs, tails, jaws, skin, and even parts of the heart and brain, with cells near a wound reverting to a stem-like state and rebuilding the missing part with perfect function. Explore the molecular signals involved, why adult mammals lost this ability, and the human medicine hoping to borrow it.

name: Axolotl Habitat
teaser: The vanishing lakes of the axolotl

exploreAction.instruction: Read how axolotls once thrived in the high-altitude lakes around Mexico City, including Lake Xochimilco, where chinampa farming created ideal canals, but drainage, pollution, and introduced fish nearly wiped them out, leaving only a few hundred wild animals. Explore the captive population in the millions, the refugio projects, and the effort to restore Xochimilco.

name: Red-eyed Tree Frog Life Cycle
teaser: From egg to leaf sleeper

exploreAction.instruction: Read how red-eyed tree frogs lay eggs on leaves over ponds, hatchlings drop into the water as tadpoles within a week, grow, and climb back to the canopy as adults that sleep on leaves by day and hunt insects by night. Explore how eggs can hatch early when threatened, and the frog's famous flash coloration.

name: Frog Calls
teaser: The choruses of the night

exploreAction.instruction: Read how frogs call to attract mates, defend territory, and warn of rain, each species with a distinctive call, from the deafening roar of bullfrogs to the ultrasonic calls of some Chinese frogs and the peeps of spring peepers that signal spring's arrival. Explore the vocal sacs that amplify sound, the males that call in choruses, and how scientists identify species by ear.

name: Glass Frog Transparency
teaser: The biology of see-through skin

exploreAction.instruction: Read how glass frogs' transparent bellies let observers watch their organs, including the beating heart, and researchers found they hide red blood cells in the liver during sleep, making them far more transparent, possibly to avoid casting shadows for predators. Explore the camouflage advantage and the science of reversible transparency.

name: Lungless Salamanders
teaser: The salamanders that breathe through skin

exploreAction.instruction: Read how lungless salamanders, the largest salamander family, have neither lungs nor gills as adults, breathing entirely through their skin and mouth lining, which forces them to live in cold, wet, flowing habitats. Explore the Appalachian diversity, their thread-like bodies, and how some climb trees and even sing quietly.

name: Amphibian Decline
teaser: Why frogs are vanishing worldwide

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a third of amphibian species face extinction from habitat loss, climate change, pollution, and chytrid fungus, a skin disease that has driven dozens of species extinct and hundreds to the brink. Explore the fungus's global spread, the rescue programs raising frogs in captivity, and what frog losses mean for ecosystems.

name: Monarch Caterpillar
teaser: The striped eater of milkweed

exploreAction.instruction: Read how monarch caterpillars hatch from eggs laid on milkweed, eat only milkweed leaves, and store the plant's toxic cardiac glycosides, becoming poisonous to predators, while their black, white, and yellow stripes warn birds away. Explore their five molts, their growth from tiny to thumb-size in weeks, and the chrysalis that follows.

name: Firefly Species
teaser: The different lights of fireflies

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the world's 2,000 firefly species flash in different patterns, colors, and rhythms, from the synchronous fireflies of the Smokies that blink in unison to the blue ghosts of Appalachia that glow steadily, each pattern a private code. Explore how females choose by pattern, the species that don't flash, and the tourism drawn to synchronous shows.

name: Dragonfly Nymph
teaser: The underwater ambush predator

exploreAction.instruction: Read how dragonfly nymphs live underwater for months to years, hunting with an extendable jaw that shoots out to grab tadpoles and fish, breathing through gills in their rectum, and jetting forward by pumping water out. Explore their final molt where they climb out and split open into flying adults, and their voracious appetite that controls mosquitoes.

name: Butterfly Metamorphosis
teaser: The caterpillar-to-butterfly transformation

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a caterpillar dissolves inside its chrysalis into a soup of cells, from which imaginal discs grow the adult butterfly's wings, eyes, and legs, a transformation so complete the adult's memories may not survive. Explore the hormones timing each stage, the chrysalis breathing tubes, and how wings form and unfold.

name: Ant Colony Structure
teaser: The castes inside an anthill

exploreAction.instruction: Read how an ant colony operates with a queen laying eggs, workers divided by age into nurses, builders, and foragers, and soldiers defending, with no single ant in charge, the colony behaving as one superorganism. Explore the pheromone trails, the communication codes, and how colonies of leafcutter ants number in the millions.

name: Cicada Song
teaser: The loudest insect chorus

exploreAction.instruction: Read how male cicadas sing by vibrating membranes called tymbals, producing calls up to 100 decibels, the loudest insect sounds, to attract mates, and different species have different songs, with the sound amplified by hollow body chambers. Explore the ear-damaging volume, the females' flicking responses, and the cicada killers that hunt them.

name: Weaver Ant
teaser: The ants that sew leaves together

exploreAction.instruction: Read how weaver ants build nests by pulling leaves together and sewing them with silk produced by their own larvae, held like living glue guns, creating basketball-sized colonies in tree canopies. Explore their cooperative silk-laying chain gangs, their painful defensive bites, and their use in ancient biological pest control.

name: Beetle Diversity
teaser: The most numerous animals on Earth

exploreAction.instruction: Read how beetles make up a quarter of all known animal species, with over 400,000 described, from jewel beetles with iridescent shells to bombardier beetles that spray boiling chemicals, and their success from deserts to glaciers. Explore why they're so diverse, the beetle-collecting tradition, and the famous quote about a creator's fondness for beetles.

name: Bombardier Beetle
teaser: The beetle that sprays boiling spray

exploreAction.instruction: Read how bombardier beetles defend by mixing hydroquinone and hydrogen peroxide in a reaction chamber, shooting a boiling-hot, foul spray from their rear at 100 pulses a second, accurate enough to hit a predator's face. Explore the chemistry and the debate it once sparked, and how the spray deters everything from ants to frogs.

name: June Bug
teaser: The buzzing beetle of summer nights

exploreAction.instruction: Read how June bugs, heavy scarab beetles, clumsily bump into windows and lights on summer evenings, their grubs feeding on grass roots underground for years before emerging as adults that eat leaves. Explore why they fly into lights, their short adult lives, and how they're food for owls, skunks, and raccoons.

name: Cricket
teaser: The chirping musician of the night

exploreAction.instruction: Read how male crickets chirp by rubbing their wings together, one wing carrying a file, the other a scraper, with the chirp rate rising with temperature, letting you estimate the temperature in Fahrenheit by counting chirps in 15 seconds and adding 40. Explore the ears on their front legs, the burrows males dig to amplify calls, and the field cricket's aggression.

name: Grasshopper
teaser: The leaping musician of the meadow

exploreAction.instruction: Read how grasshoppers leap 20 times their body length with spring-loaded hind legs, hear with membranes on their abdomen, and sing by rubbing legs against wings. Explore their huge appetite that can swarm into locust plagues, their camouflage from green to brown, and the difference from crickets and katydids.

name: Locust Swarm
teaser: The desert swarm that eats everything

exploreAction.instruction: Read how desert locusts normally live solitary, but when rains trigger crowding, they transform into gregarious swarming forms, gathering billions that can strip entire regions of crops in a day, one swarm covering 1,000 square kilometers. Explore the biology of the transformation, the ancient plagues, and the control campaigns using pesticides and biopesticides.

name: Katydid
teaser: The leaf-shaped night singer

exploreAction.instruction: Read how katydids, named for their katy-did calls, are leaf-shaped insects that sing from treetops at night, with ears on their front legs, and some species mimic leaves so perfectly they even have leaf-like veins and bite marks. Explore their long antennae, their green camouflage, and their role as bird food.

name: Water Strider
teaser: The insect that walks on water

exploreAction.instruction: Read how water striders skate on the surface of ponds using hydrophobic leg hairs that trap air, distributing their weight so surface tension holds them up, and they sense ripples made by struggling insects to find prey. Explore the physics of surface tension, their dimples on the water, and the males' signaling ripples.

name: Mayfly
teaser: The insect that lives a day

exploreAction.instruction: Read how mayflies spend months or years as aquatic nymphs, then emerge as winged adults that live only hours to days, some species barely a day, with no functional mouthparts, their only purpose to mate and lay eggs. Explore their mass emergence synchrony, the fish and birds that feast on them, and their ancient 300-million-year lineage.

name: Fire Ant
teaser: The stinging invader that builds rafts

exploreAction.instruction: Read how fire ants, named for their burning stings, build colonies that survive floods by linking together into floating rafts that can drift for weeks, and their invasive spread has made them a costly pest in the US. Explore their mound building, the venom's alkaloid chemistry, and the control methods from baits to phorid flies.

name: Army Ant
teaser: The marauding colony that never settles

exploreAction.instruction: Read how army ants live in nomadic colonies of millions, raiding in swarms that flush out insects, spiders, and even small vertebrates, with queens that lay millions of eggs and colonies that bivouac in living nests of their own bodies. Explore the swarm raids, the birds that follow to catch flushed prey, and their coordinated group hunting.

name: Honeybee Waggle Dance
teaser: The dance that maps flowers

exploreAction.instruction: Read how honeybees perform a waggle dance to tell hive mates the direction and distance of flowers, the angle of the waggle relative to vertical encoding the sun's bearing, the duration encoding distance, all information decoded by following bees. Explore the studies that decoded the language, the accuracy of the distance estimates, and what the dance says about insect minds.

name: Beekeeping
teaser: The ancient partnership with bees

exploreAction.instruction: Read how beekeeping dates back thousands of years, with hives from clay pots to modern boxes, beekeepers managing colonies for honey, pollination, and wax, and wearing suits and smokers to calm bees. Explore how a hive works through the seasons, the honey harvest, and the challenge of keeping bees healthy amid pests like Varroa mites.

name: Spider Silk
teaser: The miracle material spiders spin

exploreAction.instruction: Read how spider silk is five times stronger than steel by weight and more elastic than rubber, spun as liquid protein that solidifies into fiber, with different silks for webs, draglines, and egg cases, and orb-weavers recycling their webs by eating them. Explore the attempts to farm and synthesize silk for armor and medical sutures.

name: Spider Courtship
teaser: The risky romance of spiders

exploreAction.instruction: Read how male spiders risk being eaten during courtship, so they signal with plucked web vibrations, offer prey gifts, dance with patterned legs, and some even tie females down with silk, while others like the redback perform a somersault onto the female's fangs. Explore the mating strategies, sexual cannibalism, and why males so often die young.

name: Trapdoor Spider Burrow
teaser: The silk door of the ambush spider

exploreAction.instruction: Read how trapdoor spiders line burrows with silk, build hinged lids camouflaged with soil and moss, and wait beneath, sensing vibrations through silk trip-lines to spring out and grab passing insects, then retreat and close the lid. Explore the door's construction, the spider's patience, and how long females guard their burrows.

name: Wolf Spider
teaser: The hunting spider that carries its young

exploreAction.instruction: Read how wolf spiders don't spin webs to catch prey, instead hunting on the ground with excellent eyesight, and females carry their egg sacs attached to spinnerets, then carry hatchlings on their backs for weeks. Explore their burrows and wandering hunts, their eyes arranged in three rows, and why they're common in gardens.

name: Daddy Longlegs
teaser: The harvestman that isn't a spider

exploreAction.instruction: Read how daddy longlegs, or harvestmen, are not spiders, with a single fused body, no silk glands, and no venom, feeding on decomposing matter, and their legs can detach and twitch to distract predators. Explore why they gather in clusters, the myth that their venom is deadly, and their eight very long legs.

name: Spiders vs Insects
teaser: The differences between the two

exploreAction.instruction: Read how spiders differ from insects in body plan, with two body parts instead of three, eight legs instead of six, no antennae or wings, and simple eyes, and spiders belong to arachnids with scorpions and mites. Explore the common confusion, the counting legs trick, and how both groups dominate the invertebrate world.

name: Spider Bites
teaser: The truth about dangerous spiders
