exploreAction.instruction: Read how only a few spiders worldwide have venom dangerous to humans, like the widow and recluse, with most bites harmless, and spider bite myths vastly exaggerate the danger, while insect stings and wasps cause far more medical visits. Explore the symptoms of widow and recluse bites, the antivenoms, and why doctors see so few real spider bites.

name: Mantis Camouflage
teaser: The flower that's actually a mantis

exploreAction.instruction: Read how some mantises mimic flowers so closely, like the orchid mantis whose pink-white body and lobes resemble orchid petals, that they attract pollinating insects which become their prey, while others mimic bark, leaves, and grass. Explore the ambush strategy, how predators avoid them, and the limits of their disguise.

name: Aphid
teaser: The tiny sap sucker that breeds armies

exploreAction.instruction: Read how aphids pierce plants and suck sap, multiplying so fast that a single female can produce billions of descendants in a season, giving live birth and cloning themselves, while excreting honeydew that ants farm. Explore their role as garden pests, the ladybugs and lacewings that control them, and their astonishing reproductive biology.

name: Lacewing
teaser: The delicate insect with hungry larvae

exploreAction.instruction: Read how adult lacewings are delicate green insects with lacy wings, while their larvae, called aphid lions, are voracious predators that impale aphids with hollow jaws, and some species cover themselves in debris and prey corpses for camouflage. Explore their garden benefits, their chemical defenses, and the green lacewing's ultrasonic hearing.

name: Antlion
teaser: The pit-digging ambush predator

exploreAction.instruction: Read how antlion larvae dig conical pits in sandy soil and wait at the bottom for ants to slide in, flicking sand to prevent escape, then inject digestive fluids and drink the liquefied insides. Explore the pit construction, the antlion's armor, and the adult form, a delicate lacewing-like insect that lives weeks.

name: Caddisfly
teaser: The underwater builder of armor

exploreAction.instruction: Read how caddisfly larvae build protective cases from silk and materials around them, stones, sand, twigs, and even tiny shells, each species with its own case design, and some make silk nets to filter food from streams. Explore the case architecture, their role as water quality indicators, and the adult moths they become.

name: Caterpillar
teaser: The eating machine of the insect world

exploreAction.instruction: Read how caterpillars are the larval stage of butterflies and moths, eating machines that can grow 100 times their hatching size in weeks, with silk-spinning glands, and defenses from stinging hairs to eye spots and mimicry of snakes. Explore their anatomy, the legs that become butterfly parts, and the chemical defenses some carry from their food plants.

name: Butterflies and Moths
teaser: The differences and the beauty

exploreAction.instruction: Read how butterflies and moths together form Lepidoptera, insects with wings covered in microscopic scales that create their colors, with butterflies generally day-flying with club-tipped antennae and moths night-flying with feathery antennae. Explore the exceptions to every rule, the scale structure behind iridescence, and their place in pollination and food webs.

name: Stag Beetle Fights
teaser: The jousts of the forest floor

exploreAction.instruction: Read how male stag beetles use their huge mandibles to wrestle rival males, lifting and throwing them from branches to win mating rights, while females have small jaws for chewing wood. Explore the fight rituals, the energy cost of the weapons, and how size determines the outcome of the jousts.

name: Monarch Conservation
teaser: Saving the monarch migration

exploreAction.instruction: Read how monarch butterfly numbers have fallen sharply due to milkweed loss from herbicide use, logging of Mexican overwintering forests, and climate extremes, with the eastern population dropping by over 80 percent in recent decades. Explore the plant-milkweed movement, the protected reserves in Mexico, the western population's crash, and how backyard gardens help.

name: Stick Insect
teaser: The insect that disappears as a twig

exploreAction.instruction: Read how stick insects mimic twigs so perfectly, with body segments like nodes and legs held like branches, that predators pass them by, some species swaying in the wind to complete the disguise, and the longest can reach 60 cm. Explore parthenogenesis where females lay eggs without males, their camouflage molts, and the eggs that look like seeds.

name: Leaf Insect
teaser: The insect that looks exactly like a leaf

exploreAction.instruction: Read how leaf insects mimic leaves with flattened bodies, leaf-shaped wings with veins, and even bite marks and decay spots, some species swaying like a leaf in the breeze, the ultimate camouflage in Southeast Asian forests. Explore how they avoid being eaten by birds, their defensive stillness, and their display behavior when disturbed.

name: Emperor Moth
teaser: The moth with eyespots on its wings

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the emperor moth flashes large eyespots on its hind wings to startle predators, and females release pheromones that attract males from kilometers away, some males detected at 11 km in experiments. Explore the feathery antennae that sense pheromones, the caterpillar's green body, and the short adult life without feeding.

name: Honeybee Decline
teaser: Why honeybees are struggling

exploreAction.instruction: Read how honeybee colonies have been dying at alarming rates from Varroa mites, pesticides, habitat loss, and colony collapse disorder, threatening pollination of a third of our food. Explore the role of neonicotinoids, the beekeeper losses, the native bee alternatives, and what a world without bees would cost.

name: Butterfly Garden
teaser: How to attract butterflies

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a butterfly garden provides nectar flowers for adults and host plants for caterpillars, from milkweed for monarchs to parsley for swallowtails, plus sunny basking spots, shelter, and puddling areas with moisture and minerals. Explore the plant choices, why pesticides undo the work, and the joy of watching full life cycles in your own yard.

name: Bat Echolocation
teaser: The sonar of the night sky

exploreAction.instruction: Read how bats emit ultrasonic calls up to 200 times a second and read the echoes to map their world in the dark, catching insects mid-air with pinpoint accuracy, some detecting a mosquito-sized target at 10 meters. Explore the frequency ranges, the Doppler shifts they compensate for, and how the design inspired sonar and blind-navigation aids.

name: Fruit Bat
teaser: The flying gardener of the tropics

exploreAction.instruction: Read how fruit bats, or flying foxes, feed on nectar and fruit, pollinating flowers and spreading seeds across vast distances, some with wingspans over 1.5 meters and faces like foxes. Explore their roosts of thousands, their role in regenerating forests, and the threats from hunting and habitat loss that make them conservation priorities.

name: Vampire Bat
teaser: The bat that drinks blood

exploreAction.instruction: Read how vampire bats of the Americas feed on blood, making a tiny incision with razor-sharp teeth and lapping blood with a grooved tongue, and they share food with hungry roost mates in a remarkable act of reciprocal altruism. Explore why only three bat species are vampires, their heat-sensing noses, and their saliva's anticoagulant studied for medicine.

name: Bat Caves
teaser: The million-strong roosts

exploreAction.instruction: Read how millions of bats roost in caves, from Mexican free-tailed bats emerging from Bracken Cave in tornado-like streams numbering 20 million, to hibernating bats packing crevices in winter. Explore the guano that supports cave ecosystems, the white-nose fungus crisis, and why caves are critical wildlife refuges.

name: Brown Bear
teaser: The massive omnivore of the north

exploreAction.instruction: Read how brown bears, including grizzlies, range from Europe to North America, weighing up to 700 kg in coastal Alaska where salmon fuel their growth, and hibernate for months without eating, drinking, or excreting. Explore their omnivorous appetites, their digging, their fishing, and their complex relationship with humans.

name: American Black Bear
teaser: The adaptable bear of the forests

exploreAction.instruction: Read how American black bears are the most common bear species, excellent climbers that flee up trees, with an extraordinary sense of smell and a diet from berries to garbage, and they've expanded their range while other bears shrink. Explore their cubs born in winter dens, their shyness around people, and the bear-proofing of campgrounds.

name: Giant Panda
teaser: The bamboo-eating bear

exploreAction.instruction: Read how giant pandas, bears with a carnivore's gut, survive almost entirely on bamboo, eating up to 38 kg a day, and their slow digestion means constant eating, while their famous black-and-white markings may aid camouflage and communication. Explore their solitary life, their cubs born tiny and pink, and how conservation pulled them back from the brink.

name: Red Fox
teaser: The clever adaptable hunter

exploreAction.instruction: Read how red foxes are the most widespread carnivore, found across northern continents and even in cities, with a legendary cunning, hunting by sound with ears that pin down mice under snow. Explore their dens, their omnivorous diet, their mating pair bonds, and why they thrive alongside humans.

name: Arctic Fox
teaser: The white fox of the frozen north

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Arctic foxes change color with the seasons, white in winter for camouflage and brown in summer, with fur-covered paw pads and a thick tail used as a scarf, and they follow polar bears to scavenge kills. Explore their burrows that can be centuries old, their endurance of minus 50 degrees, and the lemming cycles that drive their numbers.

name: Raccoon
teaser: The masked bandit of the night

exploreAction.instruction: Read how raccoons are famous for their mask-like face markings and dexterous front paws that can open latches, jars, and doors, washing food before eating it, a behavior that gives them their name. Explore their night raids on trash cans, their city adaptation, and their den life in hollow trees and attics.

name: Skunk
teaser: The mammal with the warning spray

exploreAction.instruction: Read how skunks defend with a foul musk sprayed from glands under their tail, accurate to 3 meters and potent enough to be smelled a kilometer away, after giving unmistakable warnings by stamping and raising their tails. Explore why predators learn to avoid their black-and-white warning colors, and why skunks are beneficial pest eaters.

name: European Badger
teaser: The striped digger of the sett

exploreAction.instruction: Read how European badgers live in extended family groups called clans within vast underground setts that can have dozens of entrances and be centuries old, marking territory with latrines and scent. Explore their nocturnal foraging, their famous fights with beekeepers over hives, and the tuberculosis debate that drives culls.

name: Porcupine
teaser: The rodent with the quill defense

exploreAction.instruction: Read how porcupines are covered in up to 30,000 quills, modified hairs that detach easily and are barbed, sticking into attackers, and contrary to myth they can't shoot them. Explore the new world porcupines that climb trees with prehensile tails, their salt cravings that lead them to chew axe handles, and the predators like fishers that flip them over.

name: Marmot
teaser: The whistling rodent of the mountains

exploreAction.instruction: Read how marmots, large ground squirrels of mountains, whistle loudly to warn colonies of predators, then dive into burrows, and they hibernate for up to eight months a year, emerging to fatten on alpine plants. Explore the colonies, the sentinels that whistle, the Yellowstone species named for its calls, and their mountain meadows.

name: Beaver Lodge
teaser: Inside the beaver's dam home

exploreAction.instruction: Read how beavers build lodges of mud and sticks rising above ponds, with underwater entrances and dry chambers above water, while their dams raise water levels to flood forests for safety and food storage. Explore the engineering, the winter food caches, the young kits inside, and how a single family reshapes entire valleys.

name: Platypus Electrosense
teaser: The electric sense of the platypus

exploreAction.instruction: Read how platypuses hunt with electrosensitive receptors in their bills, sensing the tiny electrical fields of muscles twitching in hidden prey, closing their eyes, ears, and nostrils underwater to hunt entirely by electricity and touch. Explore how the bill's receptors work, the underwater head-sweeping hunting motion, and the echidna's similar but weaker sense.

name: Mountain Gorilla
teaser: The conservation comeback story

exploreAction.instruction: Read how mountain gorillas of the Virunga volcanoes dropped to around 250 individuals in the 1980s, then recovered to over 1,000 through armed ranger patrols, veterinary care, and tourism revenue, a rare conservation success against poaching and habitat loss. Explore the habituation for tourism, the life of a silverback, and the continued threats.

name: Elephant Memory
teaser: The truth about elephant memory

exploreAction.instruction: Read how elephants have exceptional memories, remembering water sources across decades of drought and individuals they met years earlier, guided by matriarchs whose knowledge keeps herds alive, and how science confirms their long-term social memory. Explore the studies of recognition, the role of the matriarch, and why elephant brains are wired for memory.

name: Elephant Trunk
teaser: The amazing anatomy of the trunk

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the elephant trunk is a fusion of nose and upper lip with up to 40,000 muscles, able to lift a log, pick a single blade of grass, snorkel, spray water, and smell water kilometers away, with a fingertip-like tip that can pluck a peanut. Explore the trunk's development in calves, its use in greeting and comfort, and the watering can technique.

name: Giraffe Neck
teaser: Why giraffes have long necks

exploreAction.instruction: Read how giraffe necks reach 2 meters to browse treetops out of reach of rivals, yet the classic competition theory has been debated, with recent research suggesting necks may have evolved for male neck-swinging fights, and their unique cardiovascular system handles the extreme height. Explore the blood pressure pumps, the valve system, and the necking combat.

name: Rhinoceros Senses
teaser: The weak eyes and sharp ears of rhinos

exploreAction.instruction: Read how rhinos have poor eyesight, barely seeing a person at 30 meters, but superb hearing that swivels their ears toward sounds and an excellent sense of smell used to read territory and detect danger. Explore why they sometimes charge humans, how their eyes are placed for grazing, and how the senses balance the blind spots.

name: Hippo Skin
teaser: The armor that sunburns

exploreAction.instruction: Read how hippo skin is up to 5 cm thick, nearly hairless, and secretes a red oily fluid that acts as sunscreen and antibiotic, the famous red sweat that isn't sweat, protecting them under the African sun. Explore the skin's sensitivity, why hippos wallow to stay wet, and how the secretion's pigments inspired sunscreen research.

name: Wildebeest
teaser: The great migration's star

exploreAction.instruction: Read how over a million wildebeest migrate in a giant loop through the Serengeti and Masai Mara, following rains and fresh grass, crossing crocodile-filled rivers in stampedes where many are lost, while calves are born in synchronized bursts. Explore the timing of the migration, the predators that follow, and the spectacle that draws the world.

name: Zebra
teaser: The striped horse of the plains

exploreAction.instruction: Read how zebras' stripes are unique like fingerprints, and scientists debate their purpose, from confusing predators and deterring biting flies to cooling and social recognition, with Grevy's zebra the largest and most endangered species. Explore their family groups, their role as pioneer grazers, and the stripes that may break up a predator's perception.

name: Gazelle
teaser: The leaping antelope of the plains

exploreAction.instruction: Read how gazelles are among the fastest and most graceful antelopes, Thomson's gazelles sprinting at 80 km/h with bounding leaps called stotting that signal fitness to predators, living on the dry plains of Africa. Explore their herding, their drought survival, and the cheetah hunts they must outrun.

name: Cape Buffalo
teaser: The unpredictable giant of the savanna

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Cape buffalo, weighing up to 900 kg, gather in large herds for protection against lions, forming circles and counter-charging predators, and are considered among the most dangerous animals in Africa when wounded. Explore their massive horns, their mud wallows, the oxpeckers that clean them, and their constant war with lions.

name: Why Okapis Have Stripes
teaser: The zebra stripes of the forest giraffe

exploreAction.instruction: Read how okapis wear zebra-like stripes on their legs and rear, likely for camouflage in the dappled light of the rainforest, breaking up their outline among tree trunks and shadows, and helping calves follow their mothers. Explore the stripe patterns that vary by individual, the similar stripes of young tapirs, and the science of disruptive coloration.

name: Aardvark
teaser: The termite eater of Africa

exploreAction.instruction: Read how aardvarks, whose name means earth pig in Afrikaans, dig into termite mounds with powerful claws and eat with a 30 cm sticky tongue, and their abandoned burrows shelter many other African animals. Explore their solitary night life, their secretive nature, and how their digging aerates the soil.

name: Tapir
teaser: The prehensile-nosed forest giant

exploreAction.instruction: Read how tapirs are large forest mammals of South America and Asia with short prehensile trunks, excellent swimmers that dive to feed on river plants, and a conservation status threatened across all four species. Explore their calves with striped coats that fade with age, their seed-spreading role, and their ancient lineage unchanged for 50 million years.

name: Deer
teaser: The antlered browsers of the woods

exploreAction.instruction: Read how deer grow and shed antlers each year, the fastest-growing tissue in the animal kingdom, used in rutting battles, and they live in herds across forests, meadows, and even suburbs. Explore the many species from whitetails to moose, the rutting season, the fawn's spotted camouflage, and their role as prey for wolves and hunters.

name: Moose
teaser: The towering giant of northern forests

exploreAction.instruction: Read how moose are the largest deer, males with palmate antlers spanning 2 meters, standing up to 2 meters at the shoulder, and they wade into lakes to feed on aquatic plants and escape flies. Explore their long legs for deep snow, their solitary nature, their defensive charges, and the car collisions that plague northern roads.

name: Elk
teaser: The bugling deer of the mountains

exploreAction.instruction: Read how elk, or wapiti, bugle with high-pitched whistles that carry across valleys during the rut, gathering harems of females, and males spar with massive antlers, while herds migrate between summer meadows and winter ranges. Explore their Yellowstone reintroduction, their role as prey for wolves, and the antler cycles.

name: Reindeer
teaser: The Arctic deer with the famous nose

exploreAction.instruction: Read how reindeer, called caribou in North America, are the only deer where both sexes grow antlers, with noses adapted to warm inhaled air and hooves that change with seasons, and they've been domesticated for thousands of years pulling sleds in the far north. Explore the migrations, the lichen diet, and the winter snow craters they dig.

name: American Bison
teaser: The comeback of the plains giant

exploreAction.instruction: Read how American bison once numbered in the tens of millions, were nearly wiped out to a few hundred by the late 1800s, and have been rebuilt through protected herds, now grazing prairies again and shaping ecosystems with their wallows and grazing. Explore their shaggy winter coats, their herd defense against wolves, and their deep cultural importance.

name: Yak
teaser: The shaggy ox of the high Himalayas

exploreAction.instruction: Read how yaks, shaggy oxen of the high Himalayas, thrive at 5,000 meters where oxygen is thin, their blood carrying more red cells, and they provide milk, meat, wool, and transport for highland herders. Explore their long bellows-like lungs, their black coats that absorb heat, and the wild yaks that still roam remote plateaus.

name: Mountain Goat
teaser: The cliff climber of the peaks

exploreAction.instruction: Read how mountain goats of North America's peaks climb near-vertical cliffs with hooves that have rough pads and sharp edges, gripping ledges no predator can follow, and nannies lead kids through dangerous terrain within days of birth. Explore their white coats, their dominance hierarchies, and the bluffs they use as refuges.

name: Alpine Ibex
teaser: The long-horned climber of the Alps

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Alpine ibex, wild goats with sweeping curved horns up to a meter long, once hunted to near extinction in Europe, rebounded through protected populations and now scale the steep faces of the Alps. Explore their incredible climbing on dams and cliffs, the horn growth rings that age them, and their comeback story.

name: Antelope
teaser: The diverse grazers of Africa

exploreAction.instruction: Read how antelope, a family including impala, kudu, oryx, and eland, range across Africa and Asia, from tiny dik-diks to eland as big as cattle, with horns on both sexes in many species and adaptations from desert survival to swamp wading. Explore their diversity of habitats, their herding, and the predators that shape their lives.

name: Impala
teaser: The leaping antelope of the savanna

exploreAction.instruction: Read how impalas leap up to 3 meters high and 10 meters long, clearing bushes and scattering in all directions to confuse predators, and they use scent glands to mark territory and alarm snorts to warn the herd. Explore their herding structure with bachelor groups and territorial males, and their place at the heart of the savanna food web.

name: Oryx
teaser: The desert antelope with the long horns

exploreAction.instruction: Read how oryx antelopes of African and Arabian deserts survive searing heat by letting body temperature rise and cooling blood in a nasal heat exchange, and their nearly meter-long horns are deadly weapons, with the scimitar oryx reintroduced to the wild after extinction there. Explore the Arabian oryx's comeback from captivity and the desert adaptations.

name: Pangolin Scales
teaser: The keratin armor of the pangolin

exploreAction.instruction: Read how pangolin scales are made of keratin like human fingernails, overlapping like roof tiles, and account for up to 20 percent of body weight, rolling into an armored ball so tight that even lions can't pry it open. Explore how the scales grow and shed, the myths of their medicinal powers that fuel poaching, and the fight to stop the trafficking.

name: Sea Otter
teaser: The tool-using keystone of the kelp forest

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sea otters float on their backs, cracking clams and urchins with stones on their chests, wrap themselves in kelp to anchor while sleeping, and their fur is the densest in the animal kingdom, a million hairs per square inch. Explore their role keeping kelp forests healthy by eating sea urchins, and their near extinction from the fur trade.

name: Walrus Haul-outs
teaser: The great gatherings on the ice

exploreAction.instruction: Read how walruses haul out by the tens of thousands on beaches and ice, with Pacific walruses forced ashore in huge numbers as sea ice retreats, creating crowding that can crush calves in stampedes. Explore why they gather, the tusks and roaring of the males, and how climate change is changing their ancient habits.

name: Humpback Bubble Netting
teaser: The cooperative fishing trick of humpbacks

exploreAction.instruction: Read how humpback whales hunt herring and krill by swimming in an upward spiral while releasing a curtain of bubbles that corrals prey into a tightening cylinder, then lunging through the middle with mouths open, sometimes working in teams. Explore the coordination, the timing, and the aerial acrobatics of the lunge.

name: Dolphin Pods
teaser: The societies of dolphins

exploreAction.instruction: Read how dolphins live in pods with complex social structures, forming alliances within alliances, babysitting each other's calves, and learning local hunting traditions like the sponge-fishing of Shark Bay. Explore the matrilineal societies, the signature whistles that act as names, and the intelligence behind their cooperation.

name: Manatee Winter Refuges
teaser: Where manatees go when it gets cold

exploreAction.instruction: Read how manatees cannot survive cold water and gather each winter in warm springs and power plant outflows in Florida, with Crystal River hosting hundreds in its 22 degree springs, and how the refuges have become tourist attractions and protected zones. Explore the cold-stress deaths, the manatee protection zones, and the seasonal gatherings.

name: The Narwhal Tusk
teaser: What the unicorn tooth is for

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the narwhal's tusk, a spiraled tooth with up to 10 million nerve endings, may sense water salinity, temperature, and pressure, with males possibly using it to assess rivals and even duel, and occasional double-tusked and female tusks exist. Explore the sensory studies, the flexing tusk, and the enduring mystery of its purpose.

name: Seal Pups
teaser: The first days of a seal's life

exploreAction.instruction: Read how seal pups are born on ice or beaches with white or golden coats, nursing milk so rich they double their weight in weeks, then abruptly weaned when their mothers return to sea, left to learn swimming and hunting alone. Explore the harp seal's white coat, the hooded seal's brief nursing, and the dangers from ice loss and predators.

name: Whale Breaching
teaser: Why whales leap from the water

exploreAction.instruction: Read how whales breach, hurling their massive bodies clear of the water and crashing back with a thunderous splash, possibly to communicate over distance, remove parasites, or simply for joy, with humpbacks the most acrobatic. Explore the energy cost, the studies of when breaches happen, and the theory that the sound carries messages across the ocean.

name: Orca Dialects
teaser: The regional languages of killer whales

exploreAction.instruction: Read how orca pods speak distinct dialects, each pod's calls passed down from mothers, with resident orcas of the Pacific Northwest each pod identified by its unique repertoire of calls, and different ecotypes like residents, transients, and offshores speaking different languages. Explore the cultural transmission, the acoustic identity, and what dialects reveal about their societies.

name: Gray Whale
teaser: The bottom-feeding traveler of the Pacific

exploreAction.instruction: Read how gray whales make one of the longest mammal migrations, 20,000 km round trip between Arctic feeding grounds and Mexican lagoons, and feed by rolling on their sides to scoop mud from the seabed, filtering amphipods through baleen. Explore the friendly whales of San Ignacio lagoon, the calf journeys, and the eastern population's recovery.

name: Blue Whale Song
teaser: The loudest sound made by any animal

exploreAction.instruction: Read how blue whale songs at up to 188 decibels are the loudest animal sounds, low-frequency pulses that can travel hundreds of kilometers underwater, with each population singing its own version of the song that slowly evolves over years. Explore the subsonic frequencies, the ship noise that drowns them out, and how hydrophone networks track them.

name: Sea Lion
teaser: The barking acrobat of the coast

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sea lions are the loud, social members of the pinniped family, with visible ear flaps and flippers they use to walk on land, gathering in noisy colonies, and they're the famous balancing performers in marine shows. Explore their swimming agility, their deep dives, and the difference from true seals.

name: Elephant Seal
teaser: The deep-diving giant with the big nose

exploreAction.instruction: Read how elephant seals dive deeper and longer than almost any other seal, past 1,500 meters for up to two hours, and males grow enormous inflatable noses and battle for harems on beaches with bloody fights. Explore the northern and southern species, their molting on beaches, and the researchers that track their oceanic wanderings.

name: Harbor Seal
teaser: The spotted seal of the coasts

exploreAction.instruction: Read how harbor seals, with spotted coats and puppy-like faces, haul out on rocky shores and sandbars along northern coasts, diving for fish and holding breath for 20 minutes, and mothers nurse pups that can swim within hours. Explore their wide distribution, their wariness of boats, and the pupping seasons on protected beaches.

name: Peacock Spider
teaser: The dancing rainbow spider

exploreAction.instruction: Read how peacock spiders of Australia are tiny jumping spiders, under a centimeter, that raise brightly colored abdominal fans and dance with coordinated leg waves to court females, each species with its own dance and colors. Explore the courtship videos that made them famous, the females' choice, and their remarkable color vision.

name: Huntsman Spider
teaser: The fast flat spider of warm homes

exploreAction.instruction: Read how huntsman spiders, with leg spans up to 30 cm, are fast, flat, and commonly found inside warm homes and cars in Australia and Asia, but their venom is mild and they help control cockroaches and other pests. Explore their sideways running, their egg guarding, and why they frighten people more than they harm them.

name: Sydney Funnel-web Spider
teaser: The dangerous spider of Sydney

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Sydney funnel-web is one of the world's most dangerous spiders, with large fangs and potent neurotoxic venom, aggressive when threatened, but no deaths have occurred since antivenom in 1981, and males roam in warm months. Explore the bite first-aid, the venom research, and the milking program that saves lives.

name: Tarantula Hawk
teaser: The wasp that hunts tarantulas

exploreAction.instruction: Read how tarantula hawk wasps, with one of the most painful stings in the insect world, hunt tarantulas, paralyzing them with a precise sting and dragging them to a burrow to lay an egg, the larva eating the still-living spider. Explore the sting rating scale, the iridescent blue-black body, and the battle between wasp and spider.

name: Cuckoo
teaser: The bird that tricks other birds

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cuckoos lay their eggs in other birds' nests, each female specializing on one host species and matching its egg color, with the cuckoo chick hatching first and pushing out the host's eggs to monopolize the foster parents' feeding. Explore the arms race with hosts that reject the eggs, and the cuckoo's hawk-like appearance.

name: Ostrich Egg
teaser: The biggest egg in the world

exploreAction.instruction: Read how ostrich eggs are the largest of any living animal, weighing up to 1.5 kg, equivalent to about 24 chicken eggs, with shells so strong an adult can stand on them, and multiple females lay in one nest for a dominant hen to incubate. Explore the egg's history as a delicacy and craft material, and how long it takes to boil.

name: Secretary Bird Kicks
teaser: The 195 Newton stomp

exploreAction.instruction: Read how secretary birds deliver kicks with up to 195 Newtons of force, five times their own body weight, delivered in less than 15 milliseconds, stunning snakes so quickly they can't strike back, before the bird finishes them with more stomps or holds. Explore the high-speed footage that measured the kicks, the accuracy of the timing, and the snake-hunting strategy.

name: Red Knot
teaser: The marathon runner of shorebirds

exploreAction.instruction: Read how red knots migrate up to 30,000 km a year between Arctic breeding grounds and southern wintering beaches, fattening on horseshoe crab eggs at Delaware Bay, a critical refueling stop, and their populations crashed when the crab harvest collapsed. Explore the epic journey, the fuel loads, and the conservation that restored the stopover.

name: Snowy Owl and Lemmings
teaser: The boom-bust cycle of the Arctic

exploreAction.targetName: Explore the snowy owl's prey cycle
exploreAction.instruction: Read how snowy owl breeding success tracks lemming populations, with owls nesting and laying more eggs in lemming boom years and skipping breeding entirely in bust years, a boom-bust cycle that also drives Arctic foxes and other predators. Explore the lemming population crashes and spikes, the owl's nomadic movements to find prey, and the irruptions south in hungry years.

name: Jacana
teaser: The bird that walks on lily pads

exploreAction.instruction: Read how jacanas walk across floating lily pads on incredibly long toes that spread their weight, earning nicknames like lily trotter, and in some species the males build the nests and incubate the eggs while females defend territory. Explore the reversed sex roles, the toes' length relative to body size, and their tropical wetland homes.

name: Cassowary Casque
teaser: The helmet on the cassowary's head

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cassowaries wear a hollow keratin casque on their heads whose purpose is debated, possibly amplifying their booming calls, protecting the head when pushing through rainforest undergrowth, or signaling age and dominance. Explore the bone and keratin structure, the calls that vibrate the casque, and the ongoing research into its function.

name: Regent Honeyeater
teaser: The bird that's forgetting its own song

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the regent honeyeater of southeastern Australia, with fewer than 400 left, is so rare that young males learn songs from other species instead of their own, producing hybrid calls, and researchers now tutor captive birds with recorded songs before release. Explore the eucalyptus woodland loss, the captive breeding program, and the urgent conservation work.

name: Lord Howe Woodhen
teaser: The flightless bird that came back from 30

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Lord Howe woodhen, a flightless rail, dropped to just 30 birds on its island, and a captive breeding program with predator control brought it back to hundreds, a celebrated recovery from the brink. Explore the island's rats and owls that devastated it, the intensive recovery work, and what the comeback proved possible.

name: Golden Lion Tamarin
teaser: The comeback of the golden monkey

exploreAction.instruction: Read how golden lion tamarins of Brazil's Atlantic forest dropped to a few hundred before a famous captive breeding and reintroduction program rebuilt their numbers, with conservationists carrying young monkeys into the forest in boxes to release them. Explore the golden mane, the family groups, and the forest corridors now connecting isolated populations.

name: Black-footed Ferret
teaser: The ferret brought back from extinction in the wild

exploreAction.instruction: Read how black-footed ferrets were declared extinct in the wild until a small colony was found in Wyoming in 1981, and captive breeding with prairie dog conservation has since released thousands back into the prairies. Explore their dependence on prairie dog towns, the genetic bottleneck, and the setbacks from disease.

name: California Condor Recovery
teaser: The 22 bird comeback

exploreAction.instruction: Read how California condors dropped to just 22 birds in 1982, all captured for a breeding program, and have since been released and now number over 500, though they still need lead-free ammunition rules and regular vet care to survive in the wild. Explore the hand puppets that raised chicks without imprinting, the release sites, and the lead poisoning threat.

name: Vaquita
teaser: The world's rarest marine mammal

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the vaquita, a small porpoise of Mexico's Gulf of California, has dropped to fewer than 20 individuals, caught as bycatch in gillnets set for the endangered totoaba fish, and faces imminent extinction without removing the nets. Explore the rescue attempts, the protected refuge, and the global campaign to save it.

name: Amur Leopard
teaser: The rarest big cat on Earth

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Amur leopards of the Russian Far East dropped to around 30 individuals, the rarest big cat, and have slowly recovered to over 100 through strict protection and habitat work, with camera traps documenting the comeback. Explore their thick winter coats, their prey of deer and boar, and the national park that anchors their survival.

name: Addax
teaser: The pale antelope of the deep Sahara

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the addax, a pale antelope with spiral horns, survives the deep Sahara with a body that barely sweats and kidneys that extract water, once common, now critically endangered from hunting and desertification, with fewer than 100 left in the wild. Explore the reintroduction programs in fenced reserves, and their historic migrations across the dunes.

name: Scimitar Oryx
teaser: The extinct-in-the-wild antelope coming home

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the scimitar-horned oryx, declared extinct in the wild in 2000, has been reintroduced to Chad from captive herds through a pioneering rewilding program, with GPS-collared herds monitored across the Sahel. Explore the desert adaptations, the herding into release pens, and the poaching and drought challenges the comeback faces.
